questions.question: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems. This team has two extraction workloads: an interactive upload flow where users wait for validation before submitting documents, and a nightly archive reprocessing job whose results are reviewed the next business day. Leadership wants to reduce token costs without degrading the user-facing flow. What should the architect recommend?

choices.text: Route interactive validation through the Message Batches API, and reserve synchronous calls for nightly archive reprocessing.
Route both workloads through the Message Batches API, and rely on typical one-hour completion for interactive validation.
Keep both workloads on synchronous Messages API calls, and avoid Batch because results may take the full processing window.
Route the nightly archive reprocessing through the Message Batches API, and keep interactive validation on synchronous Messages API calls.

explanations.A: This reverses the latency requirements of the two workloads. Synchronous calls are better suited for the user-facing path, while batch processing is designed for asynchronous large-volume work.
explanations.B: This treats a common completion time as if it were a latency guarantee. Batch processing can take up to 24 hours, so it is not appropriate for a workflow where users are waiting for immediate validation.
explanations.C: This protects the interactive flow but misses a valid cost optimization for the nightly job. The possibility of a long processing window matters much less when the downstream review happens the next business day.
explanations.D: This matches the Message Batches API tradeoff: lower cost for asynchronous workloads that can wait. The interactive validation path needs immediate feedback, while the nightly reprocessing job can tolerate delayed completion.

questions.questionExplanation: The Message Batches API is designed for asynchronously processing large volumes of Messages API requests, not for immediate interactive responses. Its main tradeoff is cost versus latency: Anthropic documents that batch usage is charged at 50% of standard API prices, but a batch can take up to 24 hours to complete. For a structured extraction system, the practical rule is to send latency-tolerant work to batch, such as nightly archive processing, offline audits, or next-day report generation. Keep blocking user flows synchronous, especially when a user is waiting to correct or submit a document based on the extraction result. The phrase “most batches complete within 1 hour” should not be treated as a service guarantee. The documented model is asynchronous completion, with results available when processing ends or after the 24-hour processing window, whichever comes first. See Batch processing and Create a Message Batch.

questions.question: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports. This team creates a reusable source-audit skill that report-generation subagents invoke before drafting final reports. The skill should inspect local templates and citation examples, but it should not be able to edit files or run shell commands when it executes. What is the best way to configure this constraint?

choices.text: Add `allowed-tools: Read Grep Glob` to the skill's `SKILL.md` frontmatter.
Move the workflow into `CLAUDE.md` with instructions to avoid edits.
Add an inspection-only warning to the skill's `description` in `SKILL.md`.
Wrap the workflow in a project slash command that requests read-only behavior.

explanations.A: The documented skill-level control is the optional allowed-tools field in the SKILL.md frontmatter. Setting it to tools such as Read, Grep, and Glob limits the tools available during that skill's execution, which matches an inspection-only workflow.
explanations.B: CLAUDE.md is persistent project context for general instructions and conventions. Moving the workflow there would make the guidance broader, but it would not create a skill-scoped tool restriction.
explanations.C: The description field is useful because Claude uses it to decide when to apply a skill. It is not the documented mechanism for constraining which tools the skill can use during execution.
explanations.D: A slash command can package a repeatable prompt or workflow for users to invoke. Asking for read-only behavior in command text remains prompt guidance, not a documented skill frontmatter tool constraint.

questions.questionExplanation: Claude Code skills are configured through a SKILL.md file that contains YAML frontmatter followed by Markdown instructions. For skill-scoped tool control, the relevant documented field is allowed-tools, which can be written as a space-separated string, comma-separated string, or YAML list, for example allowed-tools: Read Grep. The design tradeoff is between configuration-level constraint and prompt-level guidance. A description helps Claude decide when a skill is relevant, while instructions in CLAUDE.md or a slash command can steer behavior, but those are not the skill frontmatter mechanism for restricting available tools during the skill's execution. For an inspection-only research or reporting skill, allowing tools such as Read, Grep, and Glob keeps the skill focused on gathering local context without granting tools that modify files or run commands. See the official Claude Code skills documentation for the documented SKILL.md structure and allowed-tools frontmatter field.

questions.question: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and understand when to use plan mode vs direct execution. During a trial of a custom /project-release-notes command, this team gives the diff analysis, issue triage, and final synthesis agents the same full tool list: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash, WebSearch, WebFetch, and issue-tracker MCP tools. Even when the coordinator provides complete diff and issue summaries, the final synthesis agent often runs broad WebSearch and issue-tracker queries and adds unrelated items to the notes. What change best addresses the behavior?

choices.text: Strengthen the synthesis prompt to forbid exploratory searches after summaries are provided.
Restrict each agent to role-specific tools and route extra lookups through the coordinator.
Add few-shot release note examples that show synthesis using only delegated findings.
Rename broad lookup tools so their names indicate they are for research only.

explanations.A: Prompt instructions can improve behavior, but they do not remove the tempting tools from the synthesis agent's action space. The logs show the agent is already drifting from its synthesis role, so tool scoping is a stronger control.
explanations.B: This directly reduces the synthesis agent's opportunity to choose tools outside its role. If new research is genuinely needed, the coordinator can delegate it to a search or issue triage agent that has the right tool scope and instructions.
explanations.C: Few-shot examples can teach style and decision boundaries, but they still rely on probabilistic compliance. They also add token overhead while leaving unrelated lookup tools available to the synthesis agent.
explanations.D: Tool names are less important than descriptions and access control for reliable tool selection. Even with clearer names, the synthesis agent can still call tools it should not need for its core role.

questions.questionExplanation: Specialized agents work best when their tool access matches their responsibility. Giving every agent the same broad tool set increases the chance that an agent will solve the wrong problem, such as a synthesis agent trying to gather new evidence instead of combining the evidence it was given. The practical design pattern is scoped tool access: search-oriented agents get search and issue-tracker tools, analysis agents get inspection tools, and synthesis agents get only what they need to compose the final output. This improves reliability because the model's choices are constrained by architecture, not just by instructions. If a synthesis step discovers a real coverage gap, the coordinator should route that need to the appropriate agent rather than letting the synthesizer improvise with unrelated tools. Claude Code supports tool and MCP based workflows, but those capabilities should still follow least-privilege design. Learn more about Claude Code subagents at Subagents and MCP integration at MCP servers.

questions.question: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate. In production tests, the agent's first-pass case analysis lists every plausible billing or return issue, including marginal ones. Reviewers complain that all findings arrive with the same priority, so they cannot decide which should be auto-resolved, queued for human review, or used only for trend analysis. What change best supports calibrated review routing while preserving broad coverage?

choices.text: Route cases by reading a confidence value from each Messages API response object.
Instruct the initial finding pass to return only high-confidence issues with customer-impact severity labels.
Ask the agent to describe uncertainty in prose so reviewers can triage each case.
Run a separate verification pass that returns schema-constrained findings with confidence, severity, evidence, and routing fields.

explanations.A: Confidence is not a built-in Messages API response field. If confidence, risk, or severity values are needed, they must be requested from the model as generated output or represented in a structured schema.
explanations.B: Filtering during the initial finding pass reduces reviewer load, but it sacrifices recall because uncertain findings are never available to later ranking. When broad coverage matters, confidence filtering should move into a separate verification, deduplication, or ranking stage.
explanations.C: Free-form uncertainty explanations can help a human understand a case, but they are difficult to route consistently in an automated workflow. Schema-constrained output is better for stable queues, thresholding, and later calibration.
explanations.D: A separate verification pass preserves recall because the first pass can focus on coverage instead of suppressing uncertain findings. Returning structured fields such as confidence and severity makes downstream routing machine-routable and calibratable against reviewer outcomes.

questions.questionExplanation: For review routing, the useful pattern is a two-stage finding and verification flow. The first stage should maximize coverage by reporting plausible issues, while the later verification or ranking stage assigns fields such as confidence and severity so the system can prioritize human attention without losing low-confidence signals. Anthropic's prompting guidance for Claude Sonnet 5 explicitly recommends moving confidence filtering out of the initial finding step when recall matters, especially when a separate downstream verification, deduplication, or ranking stage exists. See Prompting Claude Sonnet 5. Because confidence is not a built-in Messages API field, the application should ask Claude to emit it as part of the output. For machine-routable routing decisions, use Structured outputs with a JSON schema rather than relying on free-form prose, as described in Structured outputs and the API response field discussion in Handling stop reasons.

questions.question: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems. During extraction prompt development, identical Claude Code requests behave differently depending on where developers start the session. The invoice package has a package-specific CLAUDE.md that says missing invoice identifiers must be represented as null, but some sessions do not follow it. What should the team do first to diagnose whether Claude Code is receiving the intended instructions in the current session?

choices.text: Run /memory in each affected session and compare the listed CLAUDE.md, CLAUDE.local.md, user-level, and managed policy memory files.
Move the invoice extraction rule into ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md so every developer inherits the same instruction globally.
Disable auto memory and rerun the same prompt to confirm that repository instructions are the only influence.
Rerun /init from the repository root and regenerate the project CLAUDE.md before comparing any session behavior.

explanations.A: This directly verifies which memory files Claude Code has loaded in the current session. If the package-specific file is not listed, Claude Code cannot see those instructions in that session, which explains inconsistent behavior.
explanations.B: User-level memory applies only to the individual developer and is not shared through the repository. It may mask the symptom for one person, but it does not diagnose whether the intended project or package memory is being loaded.
explanations.C: Auto memory is separate from CLAUDE.md memory, so disabling it does not show which repository files are loaded. The first diagnostic step should inspect the current session's loaded memory files rather than remove one possible context source.
explanations.D: /init is useful for creating initial project memory, but it is not the diagnostic command for inspecting what is loaded right now. Regenerating memory first can change the evidence and make the original inconsistency harder to isolate.

questions.questionExplanation: /memory is the right first diagnostic tool when Claude Code behaves differently across sessions. It shows the memory files loaded into the current session, such as relevant CLAUDE.md, CLAUDE.local.md, user-level, and managed policy memory, so the team can compare a working session with a failing one. This matters because memory loading depends on where Claude Code starts and what it has read. Claude Code walks upward from the current working directory, and nested memory files below the starting directory are lazy-loaded only when files in those subdirectories are read. A package-specific extraction rule can therefore be visible in one session and absent in another. Memory should also be treated as context, not as enforced configuration. If an extraction invariant must be guaranteed for downstream systems, use schema validation and enforcement mechanisms in addition to memory. But for diagnosing whether Claude Code can see the intended instructions, start with /memory. See Anthropic's documentation on Claude Code memory.

questions.question: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports. During evals, the document-analysis subagent is invoked through the Claude Messages API using the Anthropic client SDK tool-use API, and it must return a tool call for one of three extraction schemas: extract_academic_paper, extract_news_article, or extract_market_report. The document type is not known in advance. In 6% of runs, the subagent returns a conversational summary instead of invoking a schema tool, causing the coordinator to miss citation metadata. What change best enforces structured extraction without hardcoding a specific schema?

choices.text: Omit `tools` and prefill the assistant response with the desired JSON opener.
Set `tool_choice` to `{"type": "any"}` while providing all extraction tools.
Set `tool_choice` to `{"type": "auto"}` while providing all extraction tools.
Set `tool_choice` to `{"type": "tool", "name": "extract_academic_paper"}` for every document.

explanations.A: This may steer formatting, but it does not create a tool call for the coordinator to process. Without provided tools, Claude cannot return one of the extraction tool invocations needed for this workflow.
explanations.B: This forces Claude to use one of the provided tools while still allowing it to choose the appropriate extraction schema. It directly addresses the conversational-summary failure mode without forcing the wrong schema for unknown document types.
explanations.C: This leaves the decision to Claude, so the subagent may still respond directly in natural language. That is the default behavior when tools are provided and does not guarantee a tool call.
explanations.D: This forces a specific tool, which is useful only when the required schema is known. Because the document type is unknown, it can route news articles or market reports into the wrong extraction schema.

questions.questionExplanation: When a workflow using the Messages API tool-use interface needs Claude to produce a tool call rather than conversational text, configure tool_choice as an object in the request. The appropriate setting here is {"type": "any"}, which tells Claude it must use one of the available tools while preserving model choice among the provided schemas. This differs from {"type": "auto"}, where Claude decides whether to use a tool or answer directly. It also differs from {"type": "tool", "name": "..."}, which forces a particular tool and is only appropriate when the desired tool is already known. The practical tradeoff is between guaranteed tool use and schema flexibility. In multi-agent research, forcing one specific extractor can corrupt downstream synthesis if the source type varies, while allowing direct prose can drop structured citation fields. Using {"type": "any"} keeps the coordinator's handoff reliable without over-constraining the document-analysis subagent. For client tools, a tool-call response is handled by executing the returned tool_use content block and sending back a corresponding tool_result in a later user message. See Anthropic's documentation on implementing tool use and handling tool calls.

questions.question: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate. A customer support engineering team has an agent that collected the relevant case facts for a difficult billing dispute. The team wants to explore two different resolution strategies from that same point in the conversation. Each strategy should have its own conversation history that can be resumed later, and the original analysis thread should remain unchanged. Which approach should the team use?

choices.text: Run query() twice with continue_conversation=True in the same directory, then store the latest session output.
Run query() with resume=baseline_session_id for each strategy, then separate the outcomes using application metadata.
Enable file checkpointing before each strategy, then rely on checkpoints to create separate conversation histories.
Run query() with resume=baseline_session_id and fork_session=True for each strategy, then store each new session_id.

explanations.A: The continue_conversation option finds the most recent session in the current directory, which is useful for continuing recent work but not for branching from a specific baseline. It does not create independent histories from the same known session ID, so the explorations can contaminate the active thread.
explanations.B: Resuming the same session continues the original conversation history rather than creating a new branch. Application metadata can label outcomes, but it does not prevent both alternatives from being appended to the same session history.
explanations.C: File checkpointing is separate from session forking and is designed to track certain file modifications, not to branch agent conversation history. It would not create independent support-case transcripts that can be resumed as separate sessions.
explanations.D: This uses the Python Agent SDK session option that creates a new session from the resumed session history instead of continuing the original. Each fork receives a new session ID, so the two strategy explorations can be resumed independently while the baseline remains unchanged.

questions.questionExplanation: In the Claude Agent SDK, a session is the accumulated agent conversation history, including the prompt, tool calls, tool results, and model responses. When a team has a valuable shared baseline, such as verified customer facts and order details, resume targets that known session ID, while fork_session=True tells the Python SDK to create a new session from a copy of that history instead of continuing the original. The important mental model is that session forking branches conversation context, not business data or filesystem state. The fork receives its own new session_id, and the original session remains unchanged, so divergent approaches can be evaluated without mixing their reasoning traces. continue_conversation=True is less appropriate when the requirement is to branch from a specific known baseline because it selects the most recent session in the current directory. Resuming the same session without forking also falls short because both alternatives become part of one conversation history. File checkpointing solves a different problem, tracking certain file edits, and should not be treated as a substitute for independent agent sessions. See the official session behavior in Work with sessions, the Python option reference in Claude Agent SDK Python, and the distinction from file checkpointing in File checkpointing.

questions.question: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems. The system described above exposes client-executed tools named extract_fields, validate_record, submit_record, and create_review_ticket. Production logs show that when a required field is ambiguous, Claude sometimes guesses a value and emits submit_record without a successful validate_record result. The application then executes the requested tool call, and downstream systems receive records that should have gone to review. What change would most effectively enforce the required workflow?

choices.text: Add an application-level gate that blocks submit_record unless validate_record has succeeded for the same record.
Set tool_choice to tool for validate_record whenever the extraction prompt mentions ambiguous fields.
Stop the agent loop whenever the assistant text includes phrases such as ready to submit.
Add stronger system instructions telling Claude to create review tickets for ambiguous required fields.

explanations.A: Client-executed tools run in the application, so the application can enforce prerequisites before executing a requested tool call. Blocking submit_record until validation succeeds makes the required ordering deterministic instead of relying on Claude to always choose the right sequence.
explanations.B: Forcing a named tool can make Claude call validate_record on that turn, but it does not enforce what happens after validation. The application could still execute a later submit_record request unless it checks workflow state before executing the tool.
explanations.C: Natural language text is not the reliable control signal for a tool-use loop. The documented loop should inspect the structured stop_reason and tool_use blocks, not parse assistant wording as the primary workflow control mechanism.
explanations.D: Prompt instructions can improve behavior, but they remain probabilistic and do not guarantee compliance. The logs already show that the model sometimes bypasses the required validation and review path, so enforcement needs to occur where tool execution is controlled.

questions.questionExplanation: For client-executed tools, Claude does not perform the external operation itself. Claude emits a structured tool_use request, and the application decides whether and how to execute it, then returns a tool_result. That application boundary is the right place to enforce business-critical workflow ordering, such as requiring schema validation before submission. tool_choice is useful for steering whether Claude may, must, or must not use tools on a turn, including forcing a named tool. It is not a substitute for workflow state enforcement because it does not prove that later tool calls satisfy application-specific prerequisites. Similarly, prompt instructions and examples can guide behavior, but they cannot provide the same guarantee as refusing to execute an invalid tool request. The agent loop should be driven by structured API signals. The application sends tools, checks for stop_reason == "tool_use", executes allowed tool calls, returns matching tool_result blocks, and repeats until a non-tool stop reason such as end_turn. See How tool use works for the documented mechanics of tool requests, tool results, stop_reason, and tool_choice.

questions.question: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate. Your CI job runs a nightly support-triage check and needs Claude Code to process a prompt, write the result to standard output, and exit without waiting for a developer. The current job launches Claude Code and intermittently hangs in the runner. What change best fits this automated workflow?

choices.text: Invoke Claude Code with `claude -p "..."` or `claude --print "..."` in the job.
Add `--output-format json` to plain `claude` and parse the response from stdout.
Launch plain `claude` and add an instruction telling Claude to exit after answering.
Wrap the interactive `claude` command in a timeout and retry the job on failure.

explanations.A: The `-p` and `--print` flags run Claude Code in non-interactive mode, which is designed for scripts and CI/CD. In this mode, Claude Code processes the query, writes output, and exits instead of starting an interactive session.
explanations.B: Structured output is useful for automated consumers, but it does not by itself select non-interactive print mode. The documented automation pattern uses `-p` or `--print`, optionally combined with output-format options when structured output is needed.
explanations.C: Plain `claude` starts an interactive session, so this relies on conversational behavior rather than the CLI mode intended for automation. Prompt instructions do not change how the CLI process is invoked or whether it is interactive.
explanations.D: A timeout may prevent an infinite hang, but it treats the symptom rather than running Claude Code in the correct mode. Retrying an interactive invocation can still waste CI time and produce inconsistent pipeline behavior.

questions.questionExplanation: For automated jobs, the key distinction is between an interactive Claude Code session and print mode. The documented CLI pattern is claude -p "query" or claude --print "query", which runs the request non-interactively and then exits, making it suitable for scripts and CI/CD pipelines. Print mode also behaves like a Unix-style tool: it can read from stdin and write to stdout, so a pipeline can pass prompt content from files or earlier commands. If the support-triage job later needs machine-readable output, it can combine print mode with documented options such as --output-format json, but structured output does not replace the need to invoke non-interactive mode. The anti-pattern is trying to make an interactive session reliable by adding prompt instructions, timeouts, or retries. Those approaches do not change the CLI execution mode and can leave the pipeline dependent on behavior that was meant for a human-in-the-loop terminal session. See the Claude Code CLI usage reference and Run Claude Code programmatically for the documented automation patterns.

questions.question: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports. The document-analysis subagent has three extraction tools available: extract_metadata, extract_claims, and enrich_sources. For the first request in each document workflow, the coordinator must make the subagent call extract_metadata before any other extraction or enrichment can occur. Which configuration best fits this requirement?

choices.text: Set tool_choice to {"type": "any"} for the first document-analysis request.
Omit tool_choice and rely on the default behavior when extraction tools are supplied.
Set tool_choice to {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"} for the first document-analysis request.
Set tool_choice to {"type": "none"} until the coordinator has selected the schema.

explanations.A: This configuration requires Claude to use one of the available tools, but it does not determine which tool Claude will choose. The subagent could still select extract_claims or enrich_sources, so it does not satisfy the requirement.
explanations.B: When tools are provided, the default is auto, which lets Claude decide whether to call a tool and which tool to use. That flexibility is useful for open-ended turns, but it does not ensure extract_metadata is called first.
explanations.C: This configuration requires Claude to call the named tool rather than answering directly or selecting a different tool. It is the documented way to force a specific tool when tools are supplied in the Messages API request.
explanations.D: This configuration prevents Claude from using tools for that request. It cannot make the document-analysis subagent call extract_metadata, so it blocks rather than enforces the required first extraction step.

questions.questionExplanation: tool_choice controls whether Claude may use tools, must use a tool, or must use a specific named tool in a Messages API request that includes tools. For a workflow step that must begin with a particular extraction tool, {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"} is the precise configuration because it selects the named tool rather than leaving the choice to the model. The distinction between auto and any is a common source of design errors. auto lets Claude either answer directly or call a tool, while any requires a tool call but still lets Claude choose which provided tool to call. Neither option guarantees that the metadata extraction tool runs first. Use this mechanism as part of orchestration, not as a substitute for validation. Forcing a tool call controls selection, but downstream code should still validate that returned arguments and extracted fields meet the application’s schema and business requirements. See Anthropic’s Implement tool use documentation for the supported tool_choice options and Tool use overview for default tool-selection behavior.

questions.question: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and understand when to use plan mode vs direct execution. During a long refactoring session, this team notices that Claude Code starts contradicting earlier architectural decisions after many file reads, test outputs, and debugging turns. The team wants the next workflow change to preserve non-negotiable decisions without relying on the full transcript staying salient. What should they do?

choices.text: Increase use of prompt caching for repeated project instructions so earlier debugging turns no longer consume the active context window.
Maintain a structured project facts file with key decisions, constraints, and open questions, and have Claude Code update and reference it during the session.
Keep the complete transcript in every continuation and rely on the large context window to retain decisions from earlier in the session.
Ask Claude Code to summarize the conversation every few turns and replace all earlier decisions with the latest prose summary.

explanations.A: Prompt caching can reduce latency and cost for repeated prefixes, but cached content still counts toward the model's context window. It does not make old turns disappear from working memory or preserve changing project decisions by itself.
explanations.B: A structured facts file keeps critical information outside the progressively growing conversation transcript while still making it available when included or referenced. This mitigates context degradation because decisions and constraints are preserved explicitly instead of depending on older turns or verbose tool results remaining salient.
explanations.C: A large context window is still finite, and everything included in the request competes for attention and token budget. Long transcripts with tool results can dilute important decisions, especially when critical facts are buried among lower-value turns.
explanations.D: Summarization can reduce context usage, but repeated summarization can lose nuance and weaken important constraints over time. Replacing all critical decisions with prose summaries is risky when the team needs stable architectural commitments.

questions.questionExplanation: Long development sessions are vulnerable to context degradation: file contents, test logs, tool results, and back-and-forth discussion all accumulate in the model's working memory. Anthropic documents the context window as the model's working memory for a request, not durable memory, and notes that everything included in the request counts, including system content, messages, tool results, and output budget. See Context windows. The practical pattern is to separate critical state from ordinary conversation history. A structured project facts or scratchpad file should preserve decisions, constraints, current assumptions, and unresolved questions in a compact form that Claude Code can read and update. This works better than hoping older transcript content remains salient, because the team can deliberately keep the durable state concise, current, and easy to reintroduce after compaction or a resumed session. Prompt caching is a common distractor because it improves efficiency for repeated content, but it does not expand the usable context window. Anthropic explicitly documents that cached tokens still count toward the context window, even though usage accounting separates input_tokens, cache_read_input_tokens, and cache_creation_input_tokens. Server-side compaction can help long-running workflows by summarizing older context, but a durable facts file is still valuable for information that must not be diluted by repeated summarization. See Compaction.

questions.question: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports. This team needs issue tracker context in research reports: searching Jira epics, reading tickets, and linking cited issue IDs. It also needs a proprietary evidence-readiness workflow that maps issue labels to internal review stages and report sections. What should you recommend?

choices.text: Use a maintained Jira MCP server for standard issue operations, and build a focused custom MCP server for the proprietary workflow.
Build one custom MCP server that reimplements Jira issue operations and includes the proprietary workflow in the same interface.
Add Jira instructions to the coordinator prompt, and have the web search subagent locate issue pages through normal search.
Export Jira issues into static files before each run, and have the document analysis subagent read the exported files.

explanations.A: This approach reuses an existing integration for common Jira capabilities while limiting custom code to the team-specific behavior that outside servers cannot know. It reduces schema and API maintenance burden without forcing proprietary workflow logic into a generic connector.
explanations.B: This creates unnecessary maintenance for standard Jira operations that an existing MCP server can already expose. Custom servers are better reserved for workflows and data models that are specific to the team, not for duplicating common integrations.
explanations.C: Prompt instructions do not provide authenticated, structured access to Jira operations. Web search is also the wrong abstraction for private issue tracker data and would not reliably expose the fields and actions needed by the agents.
explanations.D: Static exports can work for one-off analysis, but they are a poor fit for reusable issue tracker access in an agentic research system. This bypasses MCP tool discovery and can leave the system with stale or incomplete issue context.

questions.questionExplanation: MCP is designed to reduce the N-by-M integration problem: rather than every application hand-writing tool schemas and execution logic for common services, a server can package those capabilities once and expose them through a standard protocol. For standard systems such as issue trackers, the maintainable default is to use an existing maintained MCP server when it covers the needed read or action operations. Custom MCP servers are still valuable, but their best use is team-specific workflow logic: private taxonomies, internal review rules, custom report transformations, or domain processes that a general connector cannot reasonably encode. In this case, separating standard Jira access from proprietary evidence-readiness logic keeps the agent tool surface cleaner and makes ownership clearer. Putting everything into one custom server increases long-term maintenance because the team must track Jira API behavior, schema changes, authentication edge cases, and their own workflow rules together. Static exports and web search also fall short because they avoid MCP's structured tool and resource model, and they are more likely to produce stale, incomplete, or inaccessible context. Learn more about MCP concepts in Anthropic's Model Context Protocol documentation and the official MCP architecture guide.

questions.question: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems. A compliance automation team’s structured extraction system includes a specialized audit_evidence_extractor tool for extracting audit findings from formal audit reports. Production logs show the tool being called for ordinary invoices and contracts whenever the documents contain phrases such as “validation required” or “compliance check,” even when no audit evidence is present. The tool description says it is for formal audit reports, while one system instruction says: “CRITICAL: You MUST use audit_evidence_extractor whenever compliance, validation, control, or audit language appears.” What change would most directly reduce this unintended tool association while preserving legitimate audit extraction?

choices.text: Rename audit_evidence_extractor to report_parser without changing descriptions or prompt wording.
Rewrite the system prompt and tool description with narrower use boundaries and ordinary wording for audit reports.
Set tool_choice to the audit_evidence_extractor tool whenever compliance language appears.
Set tool_choice to any so Claude must call one extraction tool for every document.

explanations.A: Changing only the name is unlikely to fix tool selection because descriptions and system prompt language are major parts of the decision surface. The broad instruction would still push Claude toward the tool when those terms appear.
explanations.B: This addresses the source of the overtriggering by removing broad, forceful language that associates common words with the audit tool. Tool descriptions and system prompts both influence tool selection, so clarifying when the tool should and should not be used is the highest-leverage fix.
explanations.C: This hard-codes the same broad association that is causing the misrouting. Forced tool choice is useful when a specific tool must run, but here the issue is that the trigger condition is too broad.
explanations.D: This would require a tool call but would not ensure the correct tool is selected. It can worsen the problem because Claude must choose among available tools even when the document does not need the specialized audit extractor.

questions.questionExplanation: When tools are available, Claude normally uses tool_choice: {"type": "auto"}, so it decides whether to call a tool based on how the user request maps to the tool’s described capability and the surrounding prompt context. Anthropic documents that system prompts can steer tool use, but they are not a hard guarantee, and forceful wording can lead to overtriggering. The important design lesson is that tool selection is not isolated from prompting. Anthropic constructs a system prompt from the tool definitions, tool configuration, and any user-provided system prompt, so broad terms like “validation” or “compliance” in a forceful instruction can accidentally attach common document language to a specialized tool. The better fix is to use ordinary wording, define the tool’s intended domain clearly, and include boundaries for when it should not be used. tool_choice is the right mechanism when a tool call must be required or a specific tool must be forced, but it does not solve a bad trigger condition. For this case, improving the system prompt and the tool description preserves Claude’s ability to use the audit extractor for genuine audit reports while reducing spurious calls on unrelated documents. See Anthropic’s guidance on tool use overview, implementing tool use, and system prompts.

questions.question: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and understand when to use plan mode vs direct execution. This team delegates documentation research to separate Claude Code subagents. In a recent upgrade guide, the final write-up treated a 2022 compatibility note and a 2025 release announcement as equally current because the parent conversation only received short summaries from each subagent. What change would most directly improve temporal reliability in future generated documentation?

choices.text: Require each research subagent to return schema-conformant JSON that includes source dates and a date basis for every substantive finding.
Add a CLAUDE.md instruction telling the parent agent to prefer the most recent findings when combining subagent summaries.
Have the parent agent ask each subagent for a prose recap whenever two summarized findings appear to conflict.
Enable citations for all research sources and rely on cited source locations to provide the needed temporal context.

explanations.A: This directly addresses the failure because Claude Code subagents work in isolated contexts and return only what they include in their final output. If temporal fields are required in a structured schema, the parent has the metadata needed to interpret whether a finding is current, stale, or based on a specific collection period.
explanations.B: This may encourage better synthesis, but it does not give the parent information that the subagents did not return. Because non-fork subagents have isolated context, the parent cannot reliably infer dates from source material it never received.
explanations.C: A follow-up recap can sometimes recover missing context, but it is reactive and depends on the parent noticing a conflict first. It also does not create a durable field that downstream documentation or validation logic can consistently inspect.
explanations.D: Citations help users verify where a statement came from, but the cited location format does not itself add publication or data collection dates. This also fails when strict structured output is required, because structured outputs and Anthropic citations are documented as incompatible in the same request.

questions.questionExplanation: Claude Code subagents are useful for keeping verbose research, logs, and file exploration out of the main context, but that isolation creates a tradeoff: the parent only sees the result the subagent returns. The Claude Code subagents documentation describes subagents as operating in their own context windows, so source metadata that matters for synthesis must be explicitly returned rather than assumed to remain available. For temporal interpretation, dates should be treated as provenance fields, not as optional prose. Anthropic structured outputs let you constrain a response to valid JSON matching a schema, so fields such as publication_date, data_collection_date, retrieved_at, or date_basis can be required when downstream logic depends on them, as described in Structured outputs. Citations remain valuable for verification, but search result citations identify source locations rather than supplying publication dates, and Citations documents that strict structured outputs cannot be combined with citation blocks in the same response format.

questions.question: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems. The team is adding a new document type. Claude Code must first inspect dozens of existing extractor modules, schema validators, fixture conventions, and error-handling paths. In trial runs, the main conversation fills with search and file-read output, and by implementation time it loses track of the target schema changes. Which workflow best preserves useful context while still doing discovery?

choices.text: Switch the whole task to Plan mode and let it inspect, edit, and validate files in one continuous context.
Run the searches in the main conversation, then use /compact immediately before implementing the schema and validator changes.
Delegate the exploratory search to the built-in Explore subagent with explicit scope and conventions, then implement from its summarized findings.
Create a shared slash command that imports all extractor, fixture, and schema files into the prompt before editing.

explanations.A: Plan mode is useful when Claude should propose an approach before executing, especially for complex or multi-file changes. It does not by itself isolate verbose discovery output from the main conversation the way a subagent with its own context window does.
explanations.B: Compacting can reduce accumulated context, but it is reactive after the verbose reads have already entered the main conversation. For large discovery phases, delegating the read-heavy work before context fills better preserves the main thread for decisions and implementation.
explanations.C: Explore is designed for searching and analyzing codebases without making changes, and it runs in a separate context window. The parent conversation receives the subagent's final text result rather than all intermediate search and read output, which keeps verbose discovery from consuming the main conversation context.
explanations.D: A project slash command can standardize a workflow, but importing many files into the main prompt increases the same context pressure that caused the problem. It also does not provide the read-only isolation or summarized return behavior of the Explore subagent.

questions.questionExplanation: For a multi-phase Claude Code task, broad codebase discovery and implementation place different demands on the context window. The discovery phase often produces large amounts of low-level evidence, such as file listings, grep results, and repeated source reads. The implementation phase needs the conclusions from that evidence, not every intermediate observation. The built-in Explore subagent is documented for read-only codebase discovery. It is invoked through the Agent tool, runs in a separate context window, and returns a single text result to the parent conversation. That isolation is the key context-saving mechanism: the main conversation does not see the subagent's intermediate tool calls or outputs, only the summarized result. See Claude Code subagents and Claude Code tools reference. In practice, give Explore a focused delegation prompt: what files or behaviors to investigate, what schema and validation conventions matter, and what format its summary should use. Because Explore starts with fresh isolated context and does not inherit prior conversation details, important project-specific extraction rules should be restated in the delegation prompt rather than assumed. /compact and Plan mode are useful Claude Code workflows, but they solve different problems. Compacting reduces an already large conversation, while Plan mode helps review an approach before changes. Neither is a substitute for keeping verbose, self-contained discovery out of the main thread in the first place, a pattern also recommended in the Claude Code context window guidance.

questions.question: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems. Benchmarking shows that long packets with several independent extraction concerns are slow, and the final JSON often omits one concern when another section is unusually long. Each concern uses the same packet metadata and source text, but the extraction tasks do not depend on one another until the final schema validation step. What design change best addresses the latency and coverage issue?

choices.text: Split the concerns into parallel extraction tasks, pass shared packet context to each task, then merge and validate the unified JSON.
Send the full packet to one extractor, increase its output budget, then retry whenever a required field is missing.
Disable parallel tool use, process each concern in a fixed order, then append validation notes to the final JSON.
Let each extraction task call the next task directly, share intermediate state, then return partial JSON fragments as they finish.

explanations.A: This matches the separability of the work: each extraction concern can run independently using the same source context. A final merge and validation step preserves the downstream contract while reducing latency and missed coverage from a single overloaded pass.
explanations.B: A larger output budget may reduce truncation risk, but it does not address attention dilution or uneven coverage across independent concerns. Retrying after omissions adds latency and still relies on the same monolithic extraction pattern.
explanations.C: Disabling parallelism works against the stated independence of the extraction concerns and is unlikely to improve latency. A fixed order can be appropriate for dependent or side-effecting work, but the question states that dependency only appears at final validation.
explanations.D: Direct handoffs and shared intermediate state undermine the clean separation that makes parallel work safe. Returning partial fragments as they finish also complicates result correlation and final schema validation.

questions.questionExplanation: When several extraction concerns are independent, the best orchestration pattern is to split, run, collect, then verify. Each worker should receive the shared packet context it needs, such as document metadata, relevant source text, and the target fields for its concern, rather than relying on hidden shared state. The coordinator then collects the results, resolves conflicts or gaps, and validates a single unified JSON object against the downstream schema. Claude can emit multiple tool_use blocks in one assistant turn, and the application decides whether to execute them concurrently, sequentially, or with a mixed strategy. Parallel execution is usually appropriate for independent read-only work, while side-effecting or order-dependent work should be handled more carefully. If client tools are used, every tool_use must receive a matching tool_result in the next user message, correlated by tool_use_id, so the coordinator can synthesize from a complete result set. This design also avoids a common orchestration anti-pattern: forcing one model pass to juggle too many unrelated concerns. Fan-out is not free, because parallel workers can multiply token usage, but it trades extra orchestration cost for better focus, lower wall-clock latency, and more reliable coverage when the subtasks are genuinely separable. See Parallel tool use, Handle tool calls, and Mid-conversation effort example.

questions.question: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and understand when to use plan mode vs direct execution. A documentation platform team has a custom MCP tool invoked by a shared /docs command to update architecture documentation after refactors. When the target documentation branch is protected, the tool currently returns the plain text string "operation failed," and Claude Code repeatedly retries the same update before asking the developer what happened. Which change best prevents wasted retry attempts while preserving recovery from temporary failures?

choices.text: Configure the command to retry every documentation update with exponential backoff before reporting failure.
Add a CLAUDE.md instruction telling Claude Code to stop retrying when documentation updates fail.
Return a successful empty result when the branch is protected so Claude Code can continue the workflow.
Return MCP error results with isError set and structured content that distinguishes protected-branch failures from temporary service failures.

explanations.A: Backoff is useful for transient errors, but it wastes time on non-retryable errors such as permission or policy failures. Retrying all failures uniformly ignores the distinction the agent needs to recover intelligently.
explanations.B: A project instruction can guide behavior, but it does not provide runtime information about why a specific tool call failed. Claude would still need to infer whether the failure is a protected branch, invalid input, or a temporary outage.
explanations.C: Marking a failed update as successful hides the failure from Claude and from the developer. The workflow may continue with missing or stale documentation, which is worse than an explicit, actionable failure.
explanations.D: This gives Claude enough information to choose a sensible recovery path instead of treating all failures the same. A protected branch is not fixed by repeating the identical call, while a timeout or service outage may be worth retrying with an adjusted strategy.

questions.questionExplanation: Tool failures should carry enough structured information for the agent to decide whether to retry, change inputs, escalate, or explain the limitation. A protected documentation branch is a non-retryable condition in practice because the same tool call with the same arguments will not succeed until permissions or workflow state changes. A timeout or temporary service outage is different, since retrying later or with backoff can be productive. For an MCP tool result, use the documented error indicator isError and include clear structured content or a clear message that describes the failure and the recommended next step. The important point is not that MCP defines a magic retry-control field, but that the model receives enough semantics to avoid guessing from a generic string like operation failed. If you are returning an Anthropic Messages API tool_result block directly, that surface uses is_error, while MCP tool results use isError. Prompt instructions in CLAUDE.md are useful for team conventions, but they are not a substitute for runtime error semantics from the tool itself. The tool is the component that knows whether the failure came from permissions, validation, business policy, or infrastructure. See the MCP tool result model in MCP Tools and Claude Code MCP integration guidance in Connect Claude Code to tools via MCP.

questions.question: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and understand when to use plan mode vs direct execution. A senior engineer is about to migrate a shared authorization layer used by several packages. The dependency graph is unclear, there are multiple viable designs, and prior immediate-edit attempts caused broad rewrites that were later reverted. What should the engineer do first?

choices.text: Start Claude Code in plan mode, have it inspect the affected areas, review the proposed plan, then approve an editing mode.
Use direct execution, ask Claude to update one package at a time, then revert commits if the design shifts.
Start Claude Code in acceptEdits mode, have it inspect the affected areas, then review the resulting source changes.
Switch to bypassPermissions mode, let Claude inspect and edit freely, then rely on tests to catch bad changes.

explanations.A: This is the best workflow because plan mode lets Claude research and propose changes before modifying source files. It reduces costly rework by forcing an explicit design review before the engineer chooses how editing should proceed.
explanations.B: Direct execution is better suited to simple, well-scoped changes where the approach is already clear. In this situation, the uncertain architecture and previous reverts indicate that designing first is more appropriate than iterating through avoidable source changes.
explanations.C: The acceptEdits mode can allow file edits to be accepted automatically, which is not the safest first step when the design is still uncertain. It may be useful after a plan is approved, but it does not provide the same exploration-before-editing guardrail.
explanations.D: The bypassPermissions mode is not a planning workflow and should not be used as a substitute for reviewing a design before edits. Tests are valuable, but they do not replace an upfront plan when the main risk is choosing the wrong refactoring approach.

questions.questionExplanation: Plan mode is designed for situations where changing code immediately would be risky because the design, dependencies, or scope are not yet clear. In this mode, Claude Code can analyze the codebase and write a proposed plan, but it does not edit source files until the plan is approved. This creates a useful checkpoint for complex refactors: the developer can evaluate the approach before committing to a path, give feedback, keep planning, or approve the plan and choose how edits should proceed. Approving a plan exits plan mode and switches to an editing permission mode, such as reviewing each edit manually or accepting edits, depending on the approval choice. Do not confuse plan mode with more permissive modes such as acceptEdits or bypassPermissions. Those modes address approval behavior for edits or tool use, while plan mode specifically supports analysis and design before source changes. See the official Claude Code permission modes documentation and the Claude Code common workflows guide for the documented planning workflow.

questions.question: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems. Production evaluation shows accuracy drops on 60-page packets with predictable sections such as intake forms, narrative notes, invoices, and attachments. The current single-pass extraction often captures fields within individual sections but produces duplicate entities, inconsistent totals, and occasional schema-valid JSON with incorrect relationships. Which task decomposition strategy should this team use first?

choices.text: Summarize each packet into a narrative first, then extract the required schema fields from that summary in a final pass.
Send the full packet through one expanded extraction prompt, then ask Claude to self-check the JSON before returning it.
Generate adaptive subtasks after each page, then stop when the agent determines that all required fields have been found.
Run section-level extraction passes, then run a reconciliation pass that validates schema, deduplicates entities, and checks cross-section consistency.

explanations.A: Summarizing before extraction can discard exact values, source distinctions, and edge-case details needed for reliable structured output. It may produce cleaner prose, but it weakens the evidence base for downstream validation.
explanations.B: A larger single prompt does not address the root issue of attention dilution across long, multi-section inputs. A self-check can improve some outputs, but it still asks the same pass to reason over all local and global constraints at once.
explanations.C: Dynamic adaptive decomposition is better for open-ended investigations where the required path is not known in advance. Here, the sections are predictable, so adaptive page-by-page planning adds variability without guaranteeing systematic coverage.
explanations.D: This uses a fixed sequential pipeline suited to a predictable document structure. Local extraction reduces attention dilution, while a later global pass handles relationships, duplicates, totals, and schema-level consistency.

questions.questionExplanation: For predictable complex workflows, a fixed sequential decomposition is usually more reliable than asking one prompt to do everything. In this case, extracting locally from each known section lets Claude focus on a smaller set of evidence, then a global reconciliation pass can compare entities, totals, dates, and relationships across sections. The useful mental model is local first, global second. Local passes reduce attention dilution and make failures easier to isolate, while the global pass handles constraints that only make sense after all partial extractions are available, such as deduplication and cross-section consistency. Dynamic adaptive decomposition is valuable when the next step depends on discoveries made during exploration, but predictable document packets benefit from a more controlled pipeline. A single expanded prompt and a pre-extraction summary both preserve less operational control than a decomposed workflow, and both can hide errors behind superficially valid JSON. Anthropic's agent guidance emphasizes composing model calls and tool use into workflows when the steps are knowable, and using more agentic patterns when flexibility is required. See Agent SDK and Tool use for related orchestration and structured tool interaction patterns.

questions.question: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and understand when to use plan mode vs direct execution. A healthcare analytics team's extraction job uses Claude with a strict extraction tool to convert discharge summaries into medication reconciliation records. The tool input schema is valid, but an application validator rejects some records because medication entries cite the wrong note section or omit the required source quote. The current retry prompt says only "fix the invalid JSON," and the same citation defects often reappear. What should the extraction loop do before accepting the records?

choices.text: Retry the same request with a higher temperature, then accept the first response that differs from the rejected output.
Replace the validator with broader prompt instructions, then ask Claude to be more careful with citations on every run.
Return the validator's field paths and citation failures with the original note, then retry and route unresolved cases to review.
Accept records once the strict tool input matches the schema, then rely on reviewers to find citation mistakes later.

explanations.A: Higher temperature increases variation rather than improving factual grounding or citation accuracy. A different response is not necessarily a corrected response, so the loop still needs targeted validation feedback before acceptance.
explanations.B: Prompt instructions can improve behavior, but they do not provide deterministic checks for citation completeness or source alignment. Removing validation would hide the exact failures needed for reliable self-correction.
explanations.C: This directly addresses validation and retry quality by giving Claude specific, actionable feedback about what failed. Strict tool use can make the tool input match the schema, but citation correctness still requires application validation and a targeted correction loop.
explanations.D: Schema-conformant tool input does not prove that cited text or note sections support the extracted medication record. Deferring known validator failures to reviewers wastes review capacity and accepts defects the automated loop can often correct.

questions.questionExplanation: Validation-retry loops are most useful when they turn a vague failure into precise correction context. Instead of saying only that the output is invalid, the application should send Claude the original source plus specific validator failures, such as the field path, the missing source quote, or the cited section that does not support the extracted medication. Strict tool use with strict: true constrains tool_use.input to the tool's input_schema, which reduces schema-shape failures. It does not verify semantic truth against an external document, so downstream validators remain necessary for source citations, cross-field consistency, calculations, and other domain rules. The practical pattern is generate, validate, provide targeted feedback, retry a bounded number of times, and route unresolved or ambiguous cases to human review. This design preserves the reliability benefits of structured tool inputs while recognizing that extraction quality also depends on evidence checks outside the JSON Schema. See Strict tool use and Handle tool calls.

questions.question: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports. After a refactor, generated reports now show two linked defects: citations render twice in the final report, and some evidence excerpts disappear when the synthesis subagent output is passed to the report generator. The likely cause spans the claim-source schema, the synthesis prompt, and the report template, and the acceptance test should confirm that each claim appears once with its evidence excerpt and source URL. How should this team use Claude Code to address the defects most effectively?

choices.text: Open separate cleared sessions for each defect, ask each session to edit only its assigned file, then merge results.
Skip planning and ask Claude to fix the report bugs broadly, then inspect the diff after it finishes.
Add a Stop hook that runs the acceptance test and rely on repeated blocks as the main debugging strategy.
Enter plan mode, give one detailed request covering both defects, affected areas, constraints, and verification checks before approving edits.

explanations.A: This is incorrect because the two defects are coupled through shared data flow and output expectations. Clearing and separating sessions is useful for unrelated tasks, but here it risks inconsistent assumptions between the schema, synthesis prompt, and report template.
explanations.B: This is incorrect because a vague request omits the symptom boundaries, expected fixed behavior, constraints, and verification. Direct execution is better suited to small, obvious changes whose diff can be described clearly, not uncertain multi-file failures.
explanations.C: This is incorrect because a Stop hook is a verification guardrail, not a substitute for a clear debugging prompt and planning workflow. Hook feedback can help enforce checks at the end of a turn, but relying on repeated blocking as the main strategy risks noisy iteration instead of diagnosing the shared design issue.
explanations.D: This is correct because the defects interact across the schema, synthesis behavior, and report rendering. A single detailed prompt gives Claude Code the shared context needed to reason about the coupled change, while plan mode is appropriate for uncertain, multi-file work before editing begins.

questions.questionExplanation: Claude Code is most effective when the workflow matches the dependency structure of the work. For interacting fixes, splitting the defects too early can create inconsistent edits because each session may make different assumptions about the shared interface between synthesis and report generation. A strong request should describe the observed symptoms, the likely affected areas, the constraints, what fixed means, and how to verify the result. Anthropic's Claude Code guidance recommends detailed prompts for bugs and also recommends asking Claude to run checks and iterate in the same request, which fits an acceptance test for citation and evidence preservation. Plan mode is the right starting point because the change is uncertain and spans multiple files. Plan mode lets Claude inspect the codebase and propose an approach before editing, while approval of the plan moves the workflow into an editing mode. By contrast, /clear is better for unrelated tasks or when repeated failed attempts have polluted the context, not for coupled defects that need a shared mental model. Stop hooks can strengthen verification by running checks before Claude ends a turn, but they should complement a clear debugging prompt rather than replace planning and diagnosis for a multi-file design issue. See Claude Code best practices, permission modes, and sessions.

questions.question: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and understand when to use plan mode vs direct execution. A teammate wants Claude Code to add one guard clause to a single known function so it rejects negative quantities, then run the existing unit test for that file. The relevant file path and expected behavior are already known, and no API, schema, or architectural changes are involved. What should the developer do?

choices.text: Enter plan mode first, review a plan, then approve implementation after exploration.
Switch to acceptEdits mode first, let Claude edit, then inspect the diff afterward.
Ask Claude Code to make the small change directly and run the specified test.
Start with bypassPermissions so Claude can edit and test without permission prompts.

explanations.A: Plan mode is best when the approach is uncertain, the change spans multiple files, or the developer needs exploration before editing. For a single known guard clause with a specified test, the planning step slows down a simple task without adding much value.
explanations.B: acceptEdits changes the permission behavior by allowing file edits in scope without prompting, but it is not required to choose the right workflow for a simple fix. The key decision is to skip unnecessary planning, not to change editing permissions before making a small update.
explanations.C: This is a clear, small edit where the expected diff can be described in one sentence, so planning would add unnecessary overhead. Including the unit test gives Claude Code a concrete verification signal instead of stopping when the change merely appears complete.
explanations.D: bypassPermissions auto-approves tool uses without permission prompts, but hooks and configured deny rules can still block operations. It is documented for isolated containers, VMs, or dev containers, not as a convenience mode for simple code changes.

questions.questionExplanation: For a small, well-scoped change, Claude Code is most effective when you ask for the outcome directly and include a verification step. Anthropic's best-practices guidance says plan mode adds overhead, and that if the diff can be described in one sentence, you should skip the plan and ask Claude to do it directly. Plan mode is valuable when the approach is uncertain, the work touches multiple files, or the developer is unfamiliar with the area being changed. It lets Claude read, explore, and write a plan before source edits happen, which is useful for review but unnecessary for a known guard clause in one function. Directly asking Claude Code to implement the fix does not mean bypassing permissions. In the documented default permission mode, reads run without asking, but edits, shell commands, and network requests can still pause for approval. Modes such as acceptEdits and bypassPermissions control permission behavior, not whether planning is appropriate. See Claude Code best practices for the guidance on skipping plans for small fixes and adding verification, and Claude Code permission modes for how plan mode, default mode, acceptEdits, and bypassPermissions differ.

questions.question: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate. The team needs to add a larger feature that caches refund eligibility decisions before invoking backend tools. The engineers are unfamiliar with the policy edge cases, cache invalidation risks, and failure modes around stale eligibility data. What should they do before asking Claude Code to implement the change?

choices.text: Ask Claude Code to use AskUserQuestion to gather requirements about implementation constraints, edge cases, and failure modes before planning code changes.
Ask Claude Code to create tests for common refund cache scenarios, then use failing tests to drive the implementation iteratively.
Ask Claude Code to draft a detailed implementation plan from the current codebase and proceed once the plan appears technically consistent.
Ask Claude Code to implement a conservative cache with short expiration, then inspect the diff for any missing policy or escalation behavior.

explanations.A: This uses the documented interview pattern for larger features, where Claude first surfaces design considerations instead of immediately coding from incomplete requirements. It is especially appropriate when the team knows the goal but lacks clarity on cache invalidation, stale data behavior, and escalation edge cases.
explanations.B: Test-driven iteration is valuable after the team understands what behaviors the feature must support. If key edge cases and failure modes are still unknown, the initial tests may encode incomplete or incorrect assumptions.
explanations.C: Plan mode is useful for larger changes, but a plan based only on existing code can still miss unstated domain constraints. In an unfamiliar area, Claude should first ask targeted questions so the plan reflects business rules and operational risks.
explanations.D: This starts implementation before the important design questions have been answered. A short expiration may reduce some stale data risk, but it does not establish the right invalidation strategy, tool interaction rules, or failure behavior.

questions.questionExplanation: For larger features in unfamiliar domains, the useful first move is often to have Claude ask questions before designing. The documented pattern is to let Claude interview you, using AskUserQuestion, so it can surface requirements around technical implementation, edge cases, constraints, and failure modes before it commits to a plan. This matters for a refund eligibility cache because the hard part is not only writing storage code. The system must decide when cached data is valid, what happens when policy or order state changes, how stale results affect customer outcomes, and when uncertainty should lead to escalation rather than automated refund processing. Plan mode, test-driven iteration, and diff review are all useful Claude Code workflows, but they work best after the problem has been framed correctly. Starting with implementation or tests can make Claude optimize around assumptions that nobody has validated. The interview pattern trades a little up-front time for better requirements discovery, which is especially valuable when mistakes could affect customer trust or financial outcomes. See Anthropic's Claude Code guidance on having Claude gather context before larger work in Claude Code best practices.
