questions.question: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports. This team uses Claude Code to maintain the research system's TypeScript repository. Citation-verification tests, report-rendering tests, and orchestration tests live beside implementation files across multiple top-level folders. The team wants the same testing guidance to apply only when Claude Code is working on test files, without duplicating guidance in every package. What should they do?

choices.text: Place the testing guidance in the root CLAUDE.md file so every Claude Code session receives the same instructions.
Create .claude/rules/testing.md without frontmatter, then rely on the filename to limit it to test files.
Create .claude/rules/testing.md with paths frontmatter matching the test file patterns, then place the testing guidance below it.
Add a CLAUDE.md file in each directory that contains tests, then repeat the same testing guidance in each file.

explanations.A: Root project instructions are useful for guidance that should apply broadly across the repository. In this case, the requirement is to load the testing guidance only for test-file work, so always-loaded project context is less targeted.
explanations.B: Rules without a paths field are loaded unconditionally and apply to all files. The filename can describe the rule topic, but it does not by itself path-gate the instruction to matching test files.
explanations.C: Path-scoped rule files are designed for topic-specific instructions that apply only to matching files. Using the paths field with glob patterns lets one rule cover test files across multiple directories without repeating the same guidance in many locations.
explanations.D: Directory-level instructions are tied to directory location, so this becomes difficult to maintain when test files are colocated throughout a repository. It also creates duplicate copies of the same guidance, which can drift over time.

questions.questionExplanation: Claude Code separates broadly applicable project memory from topic-scoped rules. Project instructions can live in CLAUDE.md or .claude/CLAUDE.md, while reusable rules can live under .claude/rules/. For conventions that cut across the directory tree, such as tests colocated beside implementation files, a path-scoped rule is the better fit. A Markdown rule file can include YAML frontmatter with the exact field paths, and those path patterns use glob matching, so one rule can match files by extension, directory, or a combination. Directory-level CLAUDE.md files are useful when instructions naturally follow directory boundaries, but they are awkward when the relevant files are spread across many folders. Putting everything in the root CLAUDE.md avoids duplication, but it makes the guidance apply more broadly than needed. See the official Claude Code memory documentation for the documented locations and path-scoped rule format.

questions.question: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports. Evaluation runs show that reports on unfamiliar research topics have uneven coverage: common subdomains are detailed, while less obvious but important angles are missing. Subagents usually complete their assigned work, and the team wants to improve completeness without simply increasing the number of assignments for every topic. What orchestration change would best improve research completeness?

choices.text: Have the synthesis agent fill coverage gaps from the available summaries without launching follow-up research.
Have the coordinator scout initial findings first, then create focused subagent assignments from the discovered work list.
Have the coordinator split every retrieved source into separate subagent tasks for maximum parallelism.
Have the coordinator prewrite a larger fixed list of subtasks before any subagent begins research.

explanations.A: A synthesis agent can identify gaps, but it cannot reliably create evidence that was never collected. Without follow-up research assignments, the final report may appear complete while remaining unsupported in missing areas.
explanations.B: This uses an adaptive investigation plan, where early evidence informs the next set of subtasks. It improves coverage because the coordinator can discover the relevant branches before fanning out work to specialized agents.
explanations.C: Maximizing task count is not the same as improving decomposition quality. Subtasks should be scoped to distinct concerns, components, or questions, not divided mechanically into overly small fragments.
explanations.D: A larger fixed list may cover more obvious branches, but it still cannot adapt to what the first evidence reveals. It can also waste work on irrelevant areas while continuing to miss unexpected domains.

questions.questionExplanation: For open-ended research, an effective coordinator should treat decomposition as an adaptive investigation, not just a one-time planning step. A useful pattern is to scout inline first, discover the actual work list, then fan out focused subtasks to specialized agents once the topic boundaries are clearer. This tradeoff matters because broad research topics rarely arrive with clean, known categories. If the coordinator commits to every subtask before seeing any evidence, it may overfit to obvious categories and miss branches that only appear in early search results or documents. Anthropic's Messages API orchestration example describes this hybrid approach and also notes that subtask granularity should be sized to the problem. In that example, Workflow is defined as a custom tool schema for splitting work into independent subtask prompts, rather than as a top-level Messages API parameter, while Agent SDK or Claude Code implementations should follow the orchestration mechanism documented for their supported runtime. See Build an orchestration mode for the documented Messages API orchestration pattern, including scouting before fan-out and sizing subtasks to distinct concerns rather than maximizing task count.

questions.question: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate. During an audit rollout, this team adds a required resolution record containing customer_id, order_id, action_taken, escalation_reason, and policy_basis. The current implementation asks Claude to respond with only valid JSON, but production logs still show occasional trailing prose and missing required keys, which break parsing before the case can be stored. What change would most reliably produce a schema-compliant record that application code can consume?

choices.text: Add stronger JSON-only instructions, wrap the schema in XML tags, and reject any response with prose.
Define a strict client tool for the resolution record with an input_schema and force that tool with tool_choice.
Prefill the assistant response with an opening brace and use a delimiter stop sequence.
Register a resolution-record tool but leave tool_choice on auto for normal flexibility.

explanations.A: This can improve instruction following, but it still relies on prompt compliance rather than constrained structured output. It may reduce malformed responses, but it does not guarantee schema-following JSON or prevent missing required fields.
explanations.B: This is correct because strict tool use constrains the tool name and tool input to the declared schema. Forcing the tool with tool_choice also ensures Claude actually emits the structured tool call rather than choosing a free-text response.
explanations.C: Prefill and stop sequences can steer the surface format and reduce extra commentary. They do not validate field presence, types, enum values, or nested structure against a JSON Schema.
explanations.D: A tool definition alone does not guarantee Claude will call that tool, because auto lets the model decide whether to use a tool. If the system requires a structured record every time, the call must be required rather than optional.

questions.questionExplanation: For production structured data that must be parsed reliably, prompt-only JSON is the wrong reliability layer. Anthropic documents that without structured outputs, Claude can produce malformed JSON, missing fields, inconsistent types, or schema violations, which is exactly the failure mode shown here in JSON.parse() failures. For a tool-based design, define a user or client tool in the top-level tools array with a name, description, and input_schema. Adding strict: true to the tool definition uses constrained sampling so the tool input follows the schema, and using tool_choice with any or a specific tool makes the tool call mandatory rather than optional. The mental model is that the structured record becomes the arguments to a tool_use content block, not prose that the application hopes will parse. Claude returns stop_reason: "tool_use" with one or more tool_use blocks, and the application reads the block's input as the structured payload. See Strict tool use, Implement tool use, and Structured outputs.

questions.question: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems. After Claude generates extraction schemas and validation retry logic, subtle defects still reach downstream tests, especially around ambiguous fields and inconsistent totals. The current review prompt runs in the same long session that designed the implementation and justified its choices. What change would most effectively improve the review architecture?

choices.text: Add more few-shot extraction examples to the generator prompt and skip the separate review step.
Ask the generating Claude session to review its own code after rereading its implementation rationale.
Use /compact in the generating session, then ask it to audit the schema and retry logic.
Run a separate Claude session with fresh context and provide the requirements, diff, and review checklist.

explanations.A: Few-shot examples can improve generation consistency, especially for ambiguous extraction cases and output formats. They do not replace an independent review pass for finding defects in code or logic already produced.
explanations.B: Self-review is weaker because the same session retains the reasoning that led to the original implementation choices. Re-reading the rationale can reinforce those assumptions rather than challenge them.
explanations.C: Compacting can reduce clutter in a long Claude Code session, but it does not create an independent reviewer. The review still inherits a summarized version of the generator's context and may preserve the same assumptions.
explanations.D: A separate reviewer session avoids inheriting the generator's reasoning context, prior rationales, and accumulated assumptions. This makes the review more independent and better suited to finding edge cases the generating session may have missed.

questions.questionExplanation: For review quality, the key design choice is independence of context. Anthropic's documented Claude Code pattern recommends using one Claude session as the writer and a separate fresh session as the reviewer because the reviewer is not biased toward code it just wrote. This matters for generated extraction systems because the original session may have already committed to assumptions about nullable fields, validation behavior, or conflict handling. Asking that same session to self-review can produce useful surface-level cleanup, but it is less likely to challenge its own premises. /compact and similar context-management tools are useful when a session is long or cluttered, but they are not equivalent to a fresh reviewer. A strong review setup gives the second Claude instance the requirements, relevant files or diff, and an explicit checklist, then asks it to look for edge cases, consistency problems, and failures against the intended behavior. Learn more in Anthropic's Claude Code guidance on using separate writer and reviewer sessions at Claude Code best practices.

questions.question: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports. After a web exploration phase in a Claude Code research workflow, later subagents repeatedly rerun searches that earlier subagents already completed and fail to preserve why certain sources were rejected. The coordinator receives brief outputs from the earlier subagents, but next-phase work still starts as if no exploration happened. What should the coordinator change before spawning each next-phase subagent?

choices.text: Condense prior exploration into a source-linked summary and include it in each next subagent’s delegation prompt.
Save the prior findings for the final synthesis prompt and keep next subagent delegations independent.
Spawn the next subagents normally and rely on their isolated context windows to access the parent history.
Attach complete prior subagent transcripts to every next delegation so no detail is omitted.

explanations.A: This gives the next subagent the relevant state it needs without carrying verbose exploration artifacts forward. Non-fork subagents start with fresh, isolated context, so prior findings must be passed explicitly in the delegation they receive.
explanations.B: This delays useful context until after the repeated-search problem has already occurred. Chained subagent workflows work best when Claude passes relevant context from each completed step to the next subagent that needs it.
explanations.C: This relies on a capability that normal subagents do not have. A non-fork subagent does not automatically see the main conversation history, previously read files, or earlier subagent work unless that context is included in what it receives.
explanations.D: This may preserve detail, but it defeats the context-management purpose of using subagents for verbose exploration. Full transcripts can consume substantial context in the parent and in later subagents, making synthesis less focused and more expensive.

questions.questionExplanation: Subagents are useful for multi-agent research because they can keep verbose search logs, file contents, and exploratory work out of the main conversation, then return a compact summary. The tradeoff is that a normal subagent starts with a fresh, isolated context window, so it will not automatically know what earlier subagents found, rejected, or left unresolved. The practical pattern is to create a phase summary after each exploration phase, including key findings, source links, rejection rationale when relevant, and unresolved questions. The coordinator should include that summary in the next subagent’s delegation prompt so the next phase starts from the current research state rather than rediscovering it. This matches the documented chained-workflow pattern where each subagent completes its task, returns results, and Claude passes the relevant context to the next subagent. Passing full transcripts is usually the wrong tradeoff because it preserves detail by spending large amounts of context on low-value exploration output. Keeping all prior findings only for final synthesis also misses the point of chained work, since intermediate subagents need enough context to avoid duplicated effort and preserve provenance-sensitive decisions. See Claude Code subagents for the documented behavior of isolated subagent context, summarized subagent results, and chained subagent workflows.

questions.question: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and understand when to use plan mode vs direct execution. When Claude Code runs npm test through Bash, the raw stdout often includes long dependency warnings and absolute local paths. The team wants Claude to reason from a shorter, normalized version of successful Bash results while leaving the command execution itself unchanged. What implementation should they choose?

choices.text: Configure a PostToolUse hook matching Bash that returns updatedToolOutput with the Bash result shape.
Configure a PostToolUse hook matching Bash that exits with code 2 and writes normalized stdout to stderr.
Configure a PostToolUse hook matching Bash that returns decision: "block" with a normalization reason.
Configure a PreToolUse hook matching Bash that rewrites stdout inside the incoming tool input.

explanations.A: PostToolUse runs after a tool completes successfully, and it can replace the tool output before Claude processes it by returning updatedToolOutput. Because Bash is a built-in tool with structured output, the replacement must preserve the expected result shape rather than return an arbitrary string.
explanations.B: Exit code 2 does not block PostToolUse because the tool has already completed. For PostToolUse, stderr is shown to Claude as feedback, but it does not replace the tool output that Claude receives.
explanations.C: In PostToolUse, decision: "block" is feedback rather than true blocking because the tool has already run. Claude still sees the original output unless the hook also returns updatedToolOutput.
explanations.D: PreToolUse runs before the command executes, so there is no Bash stdout available to normalize yet. It is useful for preventing or changing a tool call before execution, not for transforming a completed tool result.

questions.questionExplanation: PostToolUse is the appropriate hook event when Claude Code should transform a successful tool result after execution but before Claude reasons over that result. The hook receives the original tool arguments and the tool response, then can return updatedToolOutput to replace what Claude sees on the next model request. The important boundary is that this does not undo or prevent the tool action. If Bash already ran, the command's effects have already occurred; use PreToolUse when the goal is to stop or alter a tool call before it executes. For built-in tools such as Bash, the replacement output must match the tool's expected structured output shape. Returning a plain normalized string where Claude Code expects a structured Bash result can cause the replacement to be ignored and the original output to be used instead. See Anthropic's hook behavior and output replacement details in Claude Code hooks.

questions.question: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate. Before enabling overnight processing of 35,000 archived support transcripts through the Message Batches API, a pilot of 30 transcripts shows inconsistent disposition decisions and missing rationale fields in some outputs. A product manager proposes running the full archive now and resubmitting bad rows the next day. What should this team do next?

choices.text: Submit the full archive as one batch, review ended results, and resubmit rows whose disposition or fields are wrong.
Run the Prompt improver once on the current template, accept the revised prompt, and start the full overnight batch.
Create a representative evaluation set, refine the templated prompt against clear criteria, and rerun it before submitting the full batch.
Add stricter JSON output constraints, keep the current instructions, and use the batch results to discover decision errors.

explanations.A: The Message Batches API is appropriate for large asynchronous workloads, but using the full production workload as the first real evaluation creates avoidable rework. Batch results and validation errors are not a substitute for prompt refinement before scaling.
explanations.B: The Prompt improver can help enhance a prompt template, but it does not replace testing the revised prompt across representative cases. Anthropic recommends providing feedback and examples, then validating prompt changes rather than assuming the first improved version is ready for broad use.
explanations.C: This uses a prompt evaluation loop before scaling, which is the right way to improve first-pass success on high-volume work. A representative sample with clear criteria can reveal repeated prompt failures before the asynchronous batch run makes those failures expensive to discover and correct.
explanations.D: Structured outputs can improve downstream parseability, but schema constraints do not verify whether the agent made the right support decision. They also do not address missing decision criteria or inconsistent handling of ambiguous support cases.

questions.questionExplanation: For a large asynchronous workload, the practical goal is to maximize first-pass success before scale. Anthropic frames prompt engineering as an evaluation loop: define success criteria, build tests that mirror real inputs, iterate on the prompt, validate the new version, then ship. In this case, a representative set should include routine returns, billing disputes, explicit human requests, policy edge cases, and transcripts with messy customer language. Prompt templates make this process easier because fixed instructions are separated from variable inputs such as {{transcript}}, {{customer_history}}, or {{policy_excerpt}}. Claude Console evaluations support comparing prompt versions across test cases, which helps identify systematic failure patterns before sending thousands of independent requests through the Message Batches API. See Define success criteria, Evaluation tool, and Prompt generator. The Message Batches API is designed for large, non-immediate workloads, but each request is processed independently and validation happens asynchronously. That makes it a poor place to discover preventable prompt defects at full volume. If structured JSON is required, Structured outputs can help with format reliability, but semantic correctness still needs evaluation and validation. See Batch processing and Structured outputs.

questions.question: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and understand when to use plan mode vs direct execution. A payments platform team is replacing its homegrown authorization layer with a policy engine across API handlers, middleware, and tests. Engineers disagree about where the policy boundary should live, and the developer assigned to it is unfamiliar with several affected packages. Which workflow should they choose before implementation?

choices.text: Use direct execution so Claude Code starts editing immediately and discovers the architecture through test failures.
Select the opus model alias and let Claude Code complete the refactor through direct execution.
Enter plan mode so Claude Code researches the codebase and proposes changes for approval before editing files.
Run a custom slash command that instructs Claude Code to avoid asking questions during the refactor.

explanations.A: Direct execution is better for small, clear tasks where the implementation path is obvious. For a cross-cutting refactor with architectural uncertainty, starting edits immediately increases the risk of committing to the wrong approach before the design is reviewed.
explanations.B: Choosing a more capable model can help with difficult reasoning, but it does not create a plan review boundary. The problem is not only reasoning difficulty, it is the need to research, compare approaches, and get approval before source files are edited.
explanations.C: This is the best fit because the work has multiple valid approaches, affects multiple files, and involves unfamiliar code. In plan mode, Claude Code can inspect files and propose an implementation plan, but it does not edit source files until the plan is approved.
explanations.D: A custom slash command can package a repeated workflow, but it does not provide the same built-in plan approval behavior. Avoiding questions is the opposite of what is needed when the approach is uncertain and architectural tradeoffs must be reviewed.

questions.questionExplanation: Plan mode is designed for work where it is valuable to separate investigation from implementation. In Claude Code, plan is a documented permission mode where Claude can research the codebase, may run exploratory shell commands subject to normal permission flow, and writes a plan before source edits occur. The key operational boundary is that Claude Code does not edit source files until the plan is approved. Anthropic's best-practices guidance recommends planning when the user is uncertain about the approach, the change modifies multiple files, or the user is unfamiliar with the code being changed. Those conditions are all present in this refactor, so direct execution is a poor fit even if it might be faster for small fixes. Selecting a stronger model can help Claude reason through difficult code, but model choice does not replace the workflow control and approval boundary provided by plan mode. See the official documentation for Claude Code permission modes, Claude Code best practices, and Claude Code model configuration.

questions.question: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and understand when to use plan mode vs direct execution. The /release-note command sends a pull request diff to Claude and needs a typed object containing fields such as title, risk_level, testing_summary, and breaking_change. The prototype asks Claude to return JSON and then parses the assistant text, but failures occur when Claude includes commentary before the JSON. Which implementation change best improves reliability while preserving a schema-based extraction contract?

choices.text: Declare a client extraction tool with an input_schema for the release note fields, require that tool call, and read the tool_use input object.
Store the release note schema in CLAUDE.md, ask the slash command to follow it, and parse the final assistant text.
Keep the text JSON prompt, prefill the assistant with an opening brace, and parse the first balanced object from the assistant text.
Execute a local extraction function after Claude requests the tool, send a tool_result, and parse the follow-up assistant text.

explanations.A: A client tool definition lets the application provide a JSON Schema through input_schema, so Claude emits structured arguments in a tool_use block. For extraction, the structured data should be read from the tool_use block's input object rather than from any free-form assistant text.
explanations.B: Project instructions can provide useful context, but they do not define a top-level tools request parameter or create a tool_use response. This approach still relies on parsing free-form assistant text, which is the source of the observed failures.
explanations.C: Assistant prefilling can improve formatting, but it still treats structured data as generated text. It does not give the application the documented tool_use block with an input object expected to conform to an input_schema.
explanations.D: For user-defined client tools, Claude emits a structured request and the application normally executes the requested operation when the tool represents an action. For a pure extraction tool, the extracted fields are already in the tool_use input object, so parsing a later assistant message adds an unnecessary and less reliable text dependency.

questions.questionExplanation: For schema-based extraction, the stronger pattern is to model the desired output as a client tool: define a tool in the top-level tools request parameter with a clear name, description, and input_schema. When Claude calls that tool, the response has stop_reason: "tool_use" and includes one or more tool_use content blocks containing id, name, and input. The extraction payload lives in input, not in the surrounding prose. This design separates human-readable explanation from machine-readable data. Claude may still include natural-language text blocks before a tool call, so production code should not scrape wording, markdown fences, or the final assistant message for the object. The application should locate the relevant tool_use block and deserialize its input object according to the schema it supplied. See Implement tool use, How tool use works, and Handle tool calls.

questions.question: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems. This team asks Claude to review a 42-file extraction pipeline in a single pass, including parsers, normalization rules, JSON schemas, validators, and downstream mapping code. Recent reviews are inconsistent: some obvious defects are found, while other issues are missed depending on which part of the pipeline dominates the review. What review design should the team adopt?

choices.text: Run only a cross-file integration review that traces extracted fields from parsing through validation and downstream export.
Run focused per-file review passes first, then run a separate integration pass over the summarized local findings and cross-file data flow.
Run several independent full-pipeline reviews in parallel, then merge all findings that appear in at least two review outputs.
Run one larger review prompt that includes every file, all requirements, and a stricter instruction to identify every possible defect.

explanations.A: This improves attention on data flow, but it drops the dedicated local review needed to catch file-specific schema, validation, and normalization defects. Cross-file tracing is complementary to per-file passes, not a replacement for them.
explanations.B: This separates local correctness checks from cross-file reasoning, which reduces attention dilution in a large review. The integration pass can focus on how extracted fields move through normalization, validation, and downstream mapping rather than re-reading every file for every issue type.
explanations.C: Parallel full reviews can increase coverage somewhat, but each reviewer still faces the same broad attention problem. Requiring duplicate findings can also suppress rare but valid defects that only one review instance catches.
explanations.D: A single undifferentiated prompt makes the model juggle local file details and cross-file interactions at the same time. Stronger wording can help clarify intent, but it does not address the core reliability problem caused by an overloaded review context.

questions.questionExplanation: For large multi-file reviews, a reliable pattern is to split the task into focused local passes and a separate integration pass. Local passes ask Claude to inspect one file or a small group of related files for issues that can be judged in that scope, such as schema constraints, nullable fields, validation behavior, and normalization rules. The integration pass has a different job: it traces how data moves across files and stages, such as parser output, normalized field names, schema validation, and downstream export mappings. This design reduces attention dilution, because Claude is not trying to inspect every line of every file while also reasoning about the full pipeline architecture. Anthropic's long-context guidance emphasizes structuring long inputs rather than placing everything into one undifferentiated prompt. In practice, that means using clear sections, preserving key findings, and placing the final task where Claude can use the organized context effectively. See Long context prompting tips for related guidance on structuring large inputs.

questions.question: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports. The document-analysis subagent extracts an evidence_type field using a JSON Schema enum of experiment, survey, expert_interview, and market_report. In testing, vague passages are often forced into a specific category, while new source types sometimes produce values outside the schema and fail downstream validation. What change best improves the schema design while preserving reliable categorization?

choices.text: Remove the enum constraint from evidence_type, and ask each subagent to write the best category label.
Add unclear and other enum values, plus an other_detail field, and instruct when to use each.
Keep the current enum list, and instruct the model to select the closest category for every passage.
Make evidence_type required and retry whenever validation fails until a listed category is returned.

explanations.A: Removing the enum makes the output more flexible, but it weakens downstream validation and can create inconsistent labels for the same concept. This trades one failure mode for another by making category normalization harder.
explanations.B: This keeps the categorical field constrained while giving the model valid choices for ambiguous and unanticipated cases. The detail field preserves useful information for downstream systems without allowing arbitrary category strings that break validation.
explanations.C: Forcing every passage into the existing categories encourages misclassification when the source is genuinely ambiguous or outside the known taxonomy. This may pass schema validation, but it degrades semantic accuracy and hides uncertainty.
explanations.D: Retries can help when the model produced malformed output or a fixable schema violation, but they do not solve a taxonomy that lacks a valid category for the source. Requiring a listed category can increase fabricated certainty for edge cases.

questions.questionExplanation: A robust structured extraction schema should constrain predictable values while still representing edge cases honestly. JSON Schema enum is useful for categorical fields because it limits outputs to known values, but a taxonomy that lacks valid categories for ambiguous or novel inputs can push the model toward false precision. Adding application-defined values such as unclear and other is a schema design pattern, not a special Anthropic requirement. unclear gives the model a valid way to report insufficient evidence, while other plus an other_detail field lets downstream systems preserve information about emerging categories without accepting arbitrary strings in the primary field. Anthropic documents structured output mechanisms through Structured outputs, including JSON schema based outputs and strict tool use, and also shows JSON Schema enum usage in tool input schemas. See Structured outputs and Implement tool use.

questions.question: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate. Production traces show that when customers describe an order indirectly, the agent sends lookup_order vague phrases like “the jacket from last winter” or “the charge on my card,” even though the backend works best with exact order IDs, verified customer IDs plus date ranges, or email receipt references. Ambiguous matches are supposed to trigger clarification or escalation, not best-guess refunds, and the backend contract cannot change this sprint. What tool-design change should this team make first?

choices.text: Update the tool and field descriptions with accepted input formats, example queries, edge cases, and usage boundaries.
Add more successful order lookup examples to the system prompt while keeping tool metadata minimal.
Force lookup_order with tool_choice for order-related turns and ask the agent to inspect matches carefully.
Route all return and billing requests to lookup_order first so backend result ranking can narrow matches.

explanations.A: Tool descriptions and field descriptions are the strongest levers for helping Claude choose and call tools reliably. This change tells Claude what inputs are valid, what ambiguous cases look like, and when the tool should not be used for best-guess matching.
explanations.B: Few-shot examples can help, but they are less direct than improving the tool metadata Claude uses at tool-selection time. Keeping metadata minimal preserves the ambiguity that caused the agent to send vague phrases as lookup inputs.
explanations.C: Forcing the tool addresses whether a tool is called, not whether it is called with usable arguments. If the user’s description is ambiguous, the agent still needs boundaries that tell it to clarify or escalate instead of selecting a likely match.
explanations.D: This increases use of the tool without improving the quality of its inputs. It can make the existing failure mode worse by encouraging lookup_order calls before the agent has enough verified information.

questions.questionExplanation: For tool use, Claude relies heavily on the tool description and the descriptions inside input_schema to decide both when to use a tool and how to populate its arguments. A strong description should explain what the tool does, when to use it, when not to use it, accepted input formats, example values, expected outputs, and boundary cases such as ambiguous or missing identifiers. In this case, the backend contract already expects precise identifiers or bounded lookup criteria. Since that contract cannot change immediately, the highest-leverage fix is to make those expectations visible in the tool metadata rather than relying on the model to infer them from a broad name like lookup_order. Routing more traffic to the tool or forcing tool_choice would only make incorrect calls more frequent, while examples in the system prompt add helpful patterning but do not replace clear tool interface documentation. See Anthropic’s guidance on defining tools and schemas in Tool Use and on MCP-based integrations in Model Context Protocol.

questions.question: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and understand when to use plan mode vs direct execution. A workflow script receives a response with `stop_reason: "tool_use"` for a client-executed `run_tests` tool. The script runs the tests successfully, but Claude keeps asking to run the same tool again instead of interpreting the results. What should the script change in its next request?

choices.text: Append a user text turn with the test output, then resume the conversation with a normal user instruction.
Append a user text summary first, then include the matching tool result block later in that same turn.
Append the assistant tool use turn, then add an immediate user turn with the matching tool result block.
Append an assistant text turn with the test output, then add a user turn asking Claude to continue.

explanations.A: Plain user text can describe the test output, but it does not complete the documented tool exchange. Claude expects a tool_result block that references the original tool use ID, not an unstructured message that omits the tool result.
explanations.B: Tool result ordering is strict in the message history. Tool result blocks must immediately follow the assistant tool use message, and within the user message they must come before any text.
explanations.C: For client-executed tools, the application must preserve the assistant message that requested the tool and then send the result back as a user message. The tool result must reference the original tool use ID so Claude can connect the output to the requested action.
explanations.D: Putting the tool output in assistant text does not represent the documented client tool exchange. Claude expects a tool_result block in a user message so it can ground the next step in the actual tool output.

questions.questionExplanation: In Claude's client-tool loop, Claude does not execute your local tool directly. It returns a structured tool_use request, your application runs the operation, and the next API request includes the original conversation, the assistant message containing tool_use, and an immediate user message containing the corresponding tool_result. The important mental model is that the conversation history is the state. If the tool result is summarized as ordinary text, placed under the wrong role, or separated from the tool use request, Claude may not reliably associate the observation with the action it asked for. The tool_result.tool_use_id ties the result back to the tool_use.id, allowing Claude to reason about whether to continue debugging, call another tool, or produce the final answer. This ordering also matters operationally. The documentation specifies that tool result blocks belong in a user message, must immediately follow the assistant tool use message, and must appear before any text in that user message. See How tool use works and Handle tool calls.

questions.question: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems. The system described above now reports 99% schema-valid outputs, and most invoices, intake forms, and contracts receive high field-level confidence scores. Reviewers can inspect only a small portion of high-confidence records each week, but the team still needs to estimate production error rates and detect rare new failure patterns before further reducing review. What should the team do?

choices.text: Draw one random sample across all high-confidence records, then report only the aggregate weekly accuracy rate.
Use the Claude Console Evaluation Tool as the sole monitor, then stop manual spot checks for high-confidence records.
Review only low-confidence records and ambiguous documents, then assume high-confidence records remain accurate after validation.
Sample high-confidence records within each document type and critical field, then track reviewed error patterns by segment.

explanations.A: A single pooled sample can produce a useful broad signal, but it can mask weak performance in rare document types or specific fields. Reporting only aggregate accuracy makes it harder to find the segments where reviewers add the most value.
explanations.B: The Console Evaluation Tool is useful for prompt and test-set evaluation, not as a substitute for production sampling. Removing manual spot checks also eliminates an important source of ground truth for detecting new production failure modes.
explanations.C: Routing low-confidence and ambiguous cases to review is useful, but it does not measure hidden errors in high-confidence outputs. This approach can miss systematic overconfidence in a document type or field that appears safe in aggregate.
explanations.D: This preserves measurement coverage across segments that may behave differently, even when overall accuracy looks strong. Sampling high-confidence records specifically helps detect overconfident errors and novel patterns that low-confidence routing would miss.

questions.questionExplanation: For structured extraction systems, high aggregate accuracy can be misleading because errors often concentrate in particular document types, fields, source formats, or edge cases. A strong monitoring design samples high-confidence outputs across meaningful strata, such as document category and critical field, so the team can estimate error rates where they matter rather than relying on one blended number. The important reliability idea is that confidence is not correctness. Low-confidence routing helps prioritize obvious review candidates, but ongoing stratified spot checks of high-confidence outputs are what reveal overconfident failures and novel patterns that the model did not know to flag. Anthropic evaluation guidance emphasizes defining task-specific success criteria, using measurable metrics, and designing evals that reflect the real-world task distribution, including edge cases. It also distinguishes between code-based, human, and LLM-based grading tradeoffs, so human review should be used where it provides high-quality ground truth rather than applied uniformly to every record. See Define success criteria.

questions.question: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and understand when to use plan mode vs direct execution. This team has a custom documentation skill / slash-invoked command that updates README sections, API references, and migration notes after refactors. The command's overall acceptance rate is high, but review data shows that incorrect outputs are concentrated in a few fields, especially function signatures and migration warnings. What should the team do before reducing human review?

choices.text: Switch the command to plan mode for all documentation updates before applying changes.
Approve documentation changes when the command's file-level confidence exceeds a fixed threshold.
Require field-level confidence outputs and calibrate review thresholds using labeled validation examples.
Use aggregate acceptance rate as the release gate and sample merged outputs weekly.

explanations.A: Plan mode can improve reviewability by showing the intended approach before edits are made, but it does not measure whether specific extracted fields are reliable. It also does not provide calibrated evidence for deciding which fields can safely bypass human review.
explanations.B: A single file-level score can hide errors in high-risk fields such as function signatures while still looking acceptable overall. A fixed threshold is also uncalibrated, so it may not reflect the actual error rate for different documentation fields.
explanations.C: Field-level confidence lets the team route only the riskiest parts of a generated documentation change to reviewers. Calibrating thresholds on labeled validation examples is necessary because raw confidence values are not meaningful until they are compared against observed accuracy for each field type.
explanations.D: Aggregate accuracy can mask poor performance in specific fields or document types, which is the failure pattern already observed. Weekly sampling after merge may find problems too late and does not prioritize reviewer effort where it is most valuable.

questions.questionExplanation: For reliability-sensitive generated documentation, the useful unit of review is often the field, not the whole file. A README update may be mostly correct while still containing a wrong function signature or an unsafe migration note, so a single aggregate metric can create a false sense of readiness. The stronger pattern is to have Claude output field-level confidence alongside the generated values, then compare those confidence scores against a labeled validation set. Calibration turns confidence from a model self-report into an operational routing signal, for example sending low-confidence function signatures and ambiguous migration warnings to human review while allowing well-calibrated low-risk fields to proceed. This is a human review workflow design problem, not just a prompting mode problem. Claude Code features such as planning, skills, and repository context help with development workflows, but they do not replace segmented validation and calibrated thresholds. See Claude Code overview for how Claude Code supports development work, and Define success criteria for evaluation guidance before changing production review gates.

questions.question: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports. During a pilot, one engineer proposes letting subagents send intermediate findings directly to other subagents so they can coordinate faster without waiting for the coordinator to issue another delegation. Which design should this team choose?

choices.text: Give every subagent the same full conversation history and let each one decide which other subagent should act next.
Route follow-up work through the coordinator and require subagents to return structured final results for any additional delegation.
Create a shared scratchpad that subagents update freely and let the report generator resolve conflicts at the end.
Add a peer-messaging tool so subagents can exchange intermediate findings and request work from each other directly.

explanations.A: Sharing broad history does not create reliable orchestration, and it increases context load while blurring responsibility for decisions. Subagents run as separate conversations, so the safer pattern is to pass only the context needed for a specific delegated task.
explanations.B: This preserves the coordinator as the single control point for task routing, error handling, and provenance tracking. It also fits the subagent model where a parent receives the subagent's final result rather than observing every internal tool call.
explanations.C: A scratchpad can help preserve findings, but using it as an unmanaged communication bus weakens coordination and provenance control. Deferring conflict resolution until the report stage allows routing errors and partial failures to accumulate without coordinator-level recovery.
explanations.D: Direct peer messaging bypasses the coordinator, making it harder to maintain consistent error handling and controlled information flow. It can also hide important dependencies from the agent responsible for synthesizing and auditing the research process.

questions.questionExplanation: In a hub-and-spoke multi-agent design, the coordinator should remain the point where assignments, results, errors, and provenance are visible. Subagents can be specialized, but their outputs should flow back to the coordinator so it can decide whether to retry, launch another subagent, narrow the scope, or annotate a coverage gap. The documented subagent model supports this mental model: the Agent tool launches subagents that run in their own context window, and the parent receives the subagent's final result rather than all intermediate activity. See the official Tools reference for the documented behavior of the Agent tool. Direct subagent-to-subagent messaging may look faster, but it trades away observability and consistent policy enforcement. For research systems that must produce comprehensive, cited reports, the coordinator needs structured outputs such as claims, sources, errors, and coverage notes so it can control information flow before synthesis and reporting.

questions.question: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate. A customer support engineering team is implementing a manual Messages API client-tool loop for get_customer. An integration test shows this sequence: Claude requests get_customer, the application calls the MCP server successfully, and the next Claude turn proceeds as if no customer record was available. The request trace shows the lookup output was stored in an application log, while the next Messages API request included only the original user message and a fresh assistant prefill summarizing the lookup. What change should the team make to the manual orchestration loop?

choices.text: Insert a user clarification message before returning the lookup output, then include the result afterward.
Send the lookup output as plain text in a user message, then resume the original conversation history.
Append the lookup output as an assistant message, then ask Claude to continue from that prefilled summary.
Append the assistant tool_use response, then send a user message containing the matching tool_result block.

explanations.A: Tool results must immediately follow the assistant message that contains the corresponding tool_use request. Inserting another message between the tool request and its result can produce ordering errors and prevents the loop from following the documented protocol.
explanations.B: Plain text in a user message is a valid API construct, but it is not the documented way to return a client-tool result. The result must be a tool_result block that references the original tool_use id and appears immediately after the assistant tool_use message.
explanations.C: Assistant messages are for AI-generated content and tool_use requests, not client-executed tool results. A summary may be useful later, but it does not satisfy the Messages API tool result contract and may omit details Claude needs.
explanations.D: Claude can incorporate client-tool output only when the application returns it in the conversation context using a user message with a tool_result block. The tool_result must reference the original tool_use block's id through tool_use_id, and it must immediately follow the assistant message that requested the tool.

questions.questionExplanation: For client tools, Claude does not execute the backend operation itself. Claude emits a structured tool_use request, your application performs the operation, and the next request must include the result as a tool_result so Claude can reason over the new information. The result belongs in a user message, not in an assistant prefill, not in an application log, and not in a separate tool role. The message ordering is part of the contract. The application should preserve the assistant response containing the tool_use block, then immediately add a user message whose tool_result references the original id as tool_use_id. Only after that can the loop call Claude again and let the model incorporate the customer record into the next reasoning step. This pattern is central to reliable agentic orchestration: observe the model's tool request, act in application code, return the observation to the model, and continue while stop_reason is tool_use. The official documentation describes the client-tool loop in How tool use works and the exact tool_use and tool_result formatting rules in Handle tool calls.

questions.question: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate. An online retailer's support engineering team wants to add a reusable /refund-audit workflow in Claude Code for reviewing changes to refund logic. It must be version-controlled with the repository, include a checklist plus example transcripts as supporting files, and prevent file modification tools or shell commands while the workflow is active. Which implementation best fits these requirements?

choices.text: Create .claude/skills/refund-audit/SKILL.md with supporting files referenced from it, and set disallowed-tools for Write, Edit, MultiEdit, NotebookEdit, and Bash.
Create .claude/commands/refund-audit.md with links to supporting files, and set allowed-tools to Read and Grep.
Create .claude/skills/refund-audit/SKILL.md with supporting files referenced from it, and set allowed-tools to Read and Grep.
Create ~/.claude/skills/refund-audit/SKILL.md with supporting files referenced from it, and set disable-model-invocation: true.

explanations.A: A project skill under .claude/skills is shared through the repository and the directory name creates the /refund-audit command. A skill directory can include supporting files, and disallowed-tools removes the specified tools while the skill is active.
explanations.B: Legacy custom command files can still create slash commands, but skills are recommended when the workflow needs supporting files and additional configuration. This also relies on allowed-tools, which pre-approves listed tools rather than blocking file modification tools or shell commands.
explanations.C: This uses the right project skill structure, but allowed-tools does not restrict all other tools. It only pre-approves the listed tools while other tools remain callable according to the normal permission settings.
explanations.D: A personal skill in the user home directory applies across that user's projects and is not shared through the repository. disable-model-invocation controls whether Claude can invoke the skill automatically, but it does not prevent file modification tools or Bash while the user-invoked workflow runs.

questions.questionExplanation: For a team-shared Claude Code workflow, use a project skill under .claude/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md. The directory name normally determines the slash command, so .claude/skills/refund-audit/SKILL.md creates /refund-audit, and the skill directory can hold related checklists, examples, templates, or scripts that are referenced from SKILL.md. The important permissions distinction is between allowed-tools and disallowed-tools. allowed-tools pre-approves listed tools, but it does not make the skill read-only. To remove file modification capabilities while the skill is active, use disallowed-tools for the relevant write and edit tools, and include Bash when shell commands must also be prevented. Legacy files in .claude/commands/ still work, but skills are the recommended path because they support directories of supporting material and richer configuration. See Claude Code skills for the documented skill structure, scope rules, frontmatter fields, invocation controls, and tool permission behavior.

questions.question: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate. An online retailer's support engineering team is implementing billing dispute handling as a lower-level Messages API tool loop. After a pilot, the orchestration layer is found to map every billing dispute to the same fixed path, even though some cases need only a policy explanation, some require order lookup, and some should be escalated before any refund action. Which change best aligns the system with Claude's tool-use model?

choices.text: Route each request through an intent classifier that selects one predefined chain of support tools for that subtype.
Force the next support tool with tool_choice: {"type":"tool","name":"process_refund"} on each turn according to application-managed workflow state.
Run a stop_reason driven loop with tool_choice: {"type":"auto"} and let Claude choose tool use or a final reply each turn.
Continue calling Claude until its assistant text says the case is resolved, then stop the tool loop.

explanations.A: This replaces model-driven next-action selection with pre-authored paths. It can be useful for deterministic workflows, but it does not match the documented agentic loop where Claude decides on each turn whether and how to use tools.
explanations.B: Forcing a specific tool constrains the next assistant response, but it is output control rather than a general multi-step orchestration strategy. Used this way, the application is scripting the workflow instead of allowing Claude to decide the next action from context.
explanations.C: This approach uses Claude's default model-driven tool selection when tools are provided, so the next action can vary based on the current request and accumulated context. The application still remains responsible for executing any emitted tool_use blocks and returning matching tool_result blocks.
explanations.D: Stopping based on generated wording is an unreliable loop-control anti-pattern. Tool loops should inspect stop_reason, continuing on tool_use and exiting on non-tool-use stop reasons such as end_turn.

questions.questionExplanation: Claude tool use is designed around a model-driven loop, not a preconfigured decision tree. With tool_choice: {"type":"auto"}, which is the default when tools are supplied, Claude decides on each turn whether to call a tool or respond directly based on the user request, tool descriptions, and prior context. The application still owns client tool execution. When Claude returns stop_reason: "tool_use" with one or more tool_use blocks, the application executes the named client tools and sends back tool_result blocks matched by tool_use_id. The loop repeats while Claude continues to request tools and exits when the response has a non-tool-use stop reason, commonly end_turn. Forcing tools with tool_choice: {"type":"any"} or tool_choice: {"type":"tool","name":"process_refund"} can be useful for output control, but it should not be confused with defining multi-step branching logic. In high-ambiguity support cases, detailed tool descriptions plus a generic stop-reason loop let Claude adapt, while programmatic gates can still be added separately for critical constraints such as blocking refunds until required verification is complete. See Anthropic's documentation on tool use overview, how tool use works, handling tool calls, and implementing tool use.

questions.question: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports. The document analysis subagent must extract each article's primary funding source and provide a citation for the extracted value. In several articles, the only sponsor-like clue appears in the document title metadata supplied by the application, while the document source text contains no funding statement or other passage naming a funder. The validator rejects those records because no supporting citation is present. What should this team do?

choices.text: Increase max_tokens for the extraction call and rerun the analysis to complete the missing funding citation.
Return the funding source as unknown and include an evidence-gap note when no citable source passage supports it.
Make the funding source a required schema field and force the extraction tool before the synthesis step.
Retry the document analysis subagent with the same source and require a more exhaustive search for funding text.

explanations.A: Increasing max_tokens is appropriate when an otherwise valid response was truncated before completion. The problem here is not an incomplete response, it is that the required evidence is not present in citable source content.
explanations.B: This handles the absence of evidence rather than treating it as a recoverable formatting problem. If the source text does not contain a citable passage, the system should preserve uncertainty and avoid manufacturing a cited value.
explanations.C: A stricter schema can improve parseability, but it does not guarantee that the source contains the requested fact. Making the field required can encourage fabricated values when documents legitimately omit the information.
explanations.D: Retrying the same input can help with transient generation or formatting failures, but it cannot create a funding statement that is absent from the source text. This risks pressuring the model to infer a funder without evidence.

questions.questionExplanation: Retries are useful when the failure is about completion state or format, such as truncated output or schema violations. They are not a way to create missing evidence. When a research pipeline requires citations, the safer design is to let the extractor say unknown, unclear, or insufficient information when no supporting passage exists. Anthropic's hallucination guidance emphasizes restricting answers to provided documents, allowing Claude to say it does not know, and retracting claims that lack supporting quotes or citations. The Reduce hallucinations guidance supports designing prompts and validators that reject unsupported claims rather than retrying until a plausible answer appears. Citations also have boundaries. The Citations documentation explains that citable content comes from text inside a document's source, while fields such as title and context are passed to the model but are not used as cited content. A clue in metadata may help orient the model, but it should not be treated as citable evidence for a cited report. Structured output mechanisms help downstream systems receive valid, parseable data, but they do not solve factual grounding. The Structured outputs documentation describes schema conformance, not a guarantee that absent facts can be recovered. For evidence-sensitive extraction, schema design should include nullable fields or explicit evidence-gap fields so the system can represent absence honestly.

questions.question: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate. During a pilot using the Claude Agent SDK, a policy-research subagent sometimes reports only "search unavailable" to the coordinator. The coordinator cannot tell whether the subagent should retry, reformulate the request, narrow the scope, or treat the result as a true absence of policy, and reviewers cannot verify the evidence behind completed research. What subagent contract change would best improve reliability?

choices.text: Return structured subagent results with error codes, attempted queries, and any available source metadata.
Increase the search limit and ask the subagent to summarize only the final search status.
Escalate every search failure directly to a human before the coordinator synthesizes the case.
Retry failed searches inside the subagent and return "no matching policy" after the final attempt.

questions.questionExplanation: The coordinator's problem is an information-poor return value: "search unavailable" carries no error class, no record of what was attempted, and no evidence trail. Anthropic's tool-design guidance says to "prompt-engineer your error responses to clearly communicate specific and actionable improvements, rather than opaque error codes or tracebacks" and to "return only high signal information back to agents," which for a subagent contract means structured results carrying an error code, the queries attempted, and any source metadata. With that, the coordinator can decide between retry, reformulation, narrowing, or true absence of policy, and reviewers can audit the evidence behind completed research. B is wrong because a higher search limit does not fix the contract, and summarizing only the final status discards the very details the coordinator and reviewers need. C is wrong because escalating every search failure to a human destroys first-contact resolution and treats transient errors as unrecoverable. D is wrong because retrying internally and returning "no matching policy" actively misreports an infrastructure failure as a substantive finding, which is worse than the current ambiguity. Reference: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents

questions.question: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports. After several runs, the final reports contain polished summaries but weak citation coverage. The web and document subagents return useful source details to the coordinator, but the synthesis subagent is invoked later with only a brief instruction to produce themes and recommendations. What change would best improve the orchestration design?

choices.text: Broaden the synthesis subagent's description so automatic routing selects it after research completes.
Include the relevant findings and source metadata directly in the synthesis subagent's Agent prompt.
Convert the workflow to independent agent-team sessions with a shared task list for every report.
Allow research subagents to communicate directly so they can share source details before synthesis.

explanations.A: This is incorrect because the problem is not whether the synthesis subagent is selected. The subagent is already being invoked, but it is not receiving enough context to preserve citations and evidence from earlier research steps.
explanations.B: This is correct because a subagent starts with a fresh context and does not inherit the parent conversation history, previous tool results, or the parent system prompt. The coordinator must pass the information the synthesis subagent needs through the Agent tool prompt, ideally in a structured form that preserves source metadata.
explanations.C: This is incorrect because agent teams are a different orchestration model for multiple independent Claude Code sessions. The described issue can be solved within the coordinator to subagent pattern by improving what the coordinator passes to the synthesis worker.
explanations.D: This is incorrect for the documented subagent pattern because subagents report results back to the main agent or caller. Direct inter-agent messaging is associated with agent teams, not the single-session coordinator to worker subagent pattern.

questions.questionExplanation: In a coordinator to worker design, the coordinator is responsible for routing information, not just routing tasks. Subagents are useful because they have their own context windows and can keep intermediate search, log, or file output from flooding the parent conversation, but that isolation also means the coordinator must explicitly provide the context needed for downstream work. The key mental model is that a synthesis subagent cannot rely on having seen what the web search or document analysis subagents saw. The parent to subagent channel is the Agent tool prompt string, so source excerpts, URLs, document names, publication dates, and any claim to source mappings should be included there when the synthesis task depends on them. This preserves provenance through the hub-and-spoke flow without switching orchestration patterns. Changing the subagent description helps Claude decide when to delegate automatically, but it does not transfer prior research findings. Likewise, direct worker to worker communication is not how documented subagents operate. The official documentation describes subagents as specialized assistants with separate contexts that return results to the main conversation, and distinguishes them from agent teams with independent sessions and inter-agent messaging: Subagents and Agent teams.

questions.question: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems. The current implementation exposes one client tool named analyze_document with parameters for document text, requested operation, and desired format. In evaluation runs, Claude sometimes uses it to produce summaries when the downstream validator expected extracted fields, and sometimes attempts claim verification without passing the source excerpt needed for validation. What redesign best improves tool selection and downstream reliability without creating unnecessary tool sprawl?

choices.text: Move the operation instructions into the system prompt and keep the same tool schema to reduce changes to the integration.
Replace analyze_document with a few non-overlapping tools for distinct workflows, each with clear descriptions, JSON Schema inputs, and minimal stable result fields.
Create a separate tool for every document field, then merge all field-level tool results into one validated downstream record.
Keep analyze_document and add more operation names to its schema enum, while requiring Claude to choose the exact operation before each call.

explanations.A: Prompt instructions can improve behavior, but they do not create distinct input contracts for different workflows. The same generic tool would still permit calls that omit task-specific data such as source excerpts for claim verification.
explanations.B: This addresses the ambiguity by making each tool represent a distinct workflow with a clear input contract. It also avoids the opposite mistake of creating many overlapping tools, which can distract the agent and make selection less reliable.
explanations.C: This overcorrects toward excessive granularity and increases the number of tools Claude must choose among. Anthropic guidance cautions that too many or overlapping tools can distract agents, so field-level tools are usually worse than workflow-level tools.
explanations.D: An enum can constrain a parameter value, but it keeps several different workflows hidden behind one broad tool. The observed failures involve mismatched purposes and missing task-specific inputs, so the tool boundary itself remains too ambiguous.

questions.questionExplanation: The best redesign is to split an overly generic tool into a small number of purpose-specific tools whose purposes do not overlap, such as extraction, summarization, and source-backed verification. Each tool should have a high-quality description explaining what it does, when to use it, when not to use it, what parameters mean, and important caveats. Anthropic documents that client tools are supplied through the top-level tools parameter with name, description, and input_schema, and that descriptions are a primary driver of tool selection. See Implement tool use. The tradeoff is important: more granular is not automatically better. A tool per field would create tool sprawl and more selection ambiguity, while one catch-all tool hides incompatible workflows behind parameters like operation or format. The useful middle ground is a few distinct tools with strong contracts and high-signal outputs, aligned with Anthropic engineering guidance on writing tools for agents. For structured extraction systems, the input_schema is the documented contract for what Claude sends when it requests a tool. If strict schema conformance for tool inputs is required, strict: true can be used with supported tool definitions to constrain tool input generation to the JSON Schema, as described in Strict tool use. Validation is still needed for downstream semantic correctness, because schema-conformant inputs do not prove the extracted facts are correct.

questions.question: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate. Pilot analysis shows the coordinator now sends refund eligibility, account access, and escalation-readiness questions to every specialist before answering. The results are accurate, but ambiguous billing cases often include unnecessary account-recovery details, and low-complexity requests consume too much context. What change best addresses the orchestration problem?

choices.text: Merge all specialist prompts into the coordinator so every issue is handled in one shared context window.
Require every specialist to return shorter summaries before the coordinator writes the final customer response.
Route each request through a coordinator step that selects only the specialists whose descriptions match the current issue.
Force the coordinator to invoke all specialists in parallel so no request waits on sequential handoffs.

explanations.A: This removes the isolation benefits that make subagents useful for specialized work and verbose intermediate output. It also increases the chance that unrelated instructions compete inside the main context.
explanations.B: Shorter summaries may reduce context usage, but they do not fix unnecessary delegation. The system would still invoke unrelated specialists, which can add irrelevant considerations and latency.
explanations.C: This preserves specialized subagents while avoiding an always-on full pipeline. A coordinator can analyze the current request, then delegate only self-contained work that is relevant to the issue being resolved.
