explanations.D: Parallel execution can reduce latency when independent work is genuinely needed, but it does not solve over-routing. Calling every specialist for every case still wastes context and can introduce irrelevant findings.

questions.questionExplanation: The core design issue is not that specialists exist, it is that the coordinator is treating the specialist set as a fixed pipeline. A better pattern is dynamic delegation: the coordinator inspects the request, identifies which work is actually needed, then invokes only the relevant subagents. This keeps specialized reasoning available for difficult returns, billing disputes, and account issues without making every customer contact pay the cost of every specialist. Subagents are most useful when a task is self-contained, can return a concise result, benefits from separate context, or needs constrained tool access. The official subagent documentation explains that each subagent runs in its own context window with its own prompt and tool permissions, and that automatic delegation is guided by the user request, current context, and the subagent description field. Clear descriptions help the coordinator choose the right worker instead of routing through all workers by habit. See Claude Code subagents. Context compression and parallelism are useful techniques, but they address different bottlenecks. Shorter summaries reduce token load after delegation has already happened, and parallel calls help when multiple independent specialists are actually required. Neither prevents irrelevant specialist outputs from influencing the final response. Merging all specialists into one prompt is the opposite tradeoff: it sacrifices isolation and makes the coordinator carry every concern in the main conversation.

questions.question: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and understand when to use plan mode vs direct execution. This team's /review command classifies pull request comments into defects, missing tests, dependency risks, and dead-code findings. In the last month, defect and missing-test comments are usually accepted, but dead-code findings are frequently dismissed because Claude flags framework entry points and reflection-based handlers that are intentionally unused by direct imports. Several developers now skim or mute the entire review output. What change should you make first?

choices.text: Increase the severity of defect and missing-test comments so developers notice the useful findings.
Measure precision and recall by finding category, then narrow or pause the noisy dead-code checks.
Combine all review categories into one quality score and tune the prompt only if that score drops.
Add a CLAUDE.md note asking Claude to be more conservative when reporting dead code.

explanations.A: Raising severity on accurate categories does not address the category that is causing developers to distrust the report. It may make the output feel more urgent, but the false-positive dead-code findings would still teach developers that the review is noisy.
explanations.B: This directly targets the trust problem by treating each review category as a classification task and identifying the category with excessive false positives. Narrowing or pausing the noisy category protects confidence in the categories that are already useful, rather than allowing one unreliable label to contaminate the whole report.
explanations.C: A single aggregate score can hide a category with a high false-positive rate when other categories perform well. This is especially risky because the practical failure is not average accuracy, it is developer trust being damaged by one visible class of bad findings.
explanations.D: A general instruction may reduce some noise, but it does not define the decision boundary for framework entry points or reflection-based handlers. Without category-level measurement and examples of what should and should not be flagged, the team cannot know whether the false-positive problem has improved.

questions.questionExplanation: The issue is not that Claude Code can never identify dead code, it is that one false-positive-heavy category can undermine confidence in the entire review surface. For developer-facing automation, trust is often categorical: if engineers repeatedly see bogus dead-code comments, they may stop reading useful defect and missing-test findings too. A reliable fix treats review findings like a classification problem. Track precision and recall by category, inspect production examples, and refine the assessment criteria for the noisy category using clear positive and negative examples. In this case, the team should distinguish genuinely unreachable code from framework entry points, reflection-based handlers, and other patterns that look unused only to a shallow import search. Anthropic's moderation guidance uses the same mental model: build examples of content that should and should not be flagged, include edge cases, and track precision and recall in production rather than relying on overall accuracy alone. The documented false-positive example, interpreting “The main actor really killed it!” as literal violence, illustrates why semantic decision boundaries matter more than keyword-like rules. See Content moderation.

questions.question: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate. While updating a repository file that defines refund triage wording, Claude Code has already read the file and an `Edit` call fails because the supplied `old_string` appears in two policy examples. The requested change applies to only one occurrence, but repeated boilerplate makes a unique exact replacement impractical. What should the team instruct Claude Code to do to make the change reliably?

choices.text: Read the current file contents, assemble the full intended file, and use `Write` to overwrite that file.
Retry `Edit` with a shorter `old_string` so Claude Code can select the closest matching occurrence.
Change `old_string` to a regex pattern that matches the target paragraph with optional whitespace.
Set `replace_all: true` on the same `Edit` call so every matching policy phrase is changed consistently.

explanations.A: This uses `Read` to obtain reliable current contents, then uses `Write` as a whole-file replacement operation. It avoids the non-unique `old_string` problem because `Write` does not depend on a unique exact substring match.
explanations.B: A shorter `old_string` is more likely to match multiple locations, not fewer. Relying on the tool to choose the closest occurrence is an anti-pattern because `Edit` requires the target string to appear exactly once unless replacing all matches is intended.
explanations.C: Claude Code `Edit` uses exact string replacement, not regex or fuzzy matching. A regex-style pattern would not solve the documented uniqueness and exact-match requirements for `Edit`.
explanations.D: This is only appropriate when every occurrence should be replaced. The situation states the requested change applies to one occurrence, so replacing both examples would modify content outside the intended scope.

questions.questionExplanation: Claude Code's Edit tool is designed for targeted exact replacement. Before an edit applies, the file must have been read in the current conversation, the old_string must match exactly, and that string must appear exactly once unless replace_all: true is intentionally used. When the intended change affects only one occurrence and a unique exact old_string cannot be constructed, the safer fallback is to use the file contents as the source of truth, construct the complete desired final file, and call Write. Write is a whole-file operation, so it bypasses ambiguous substring matching while still requiring care because it overwrites rather than appends or patches. The tempting alternatives all misuse the tool boundary. replace_all changes every matching occurrence, regex does not apply to Edit, and shorter or looser strings increase ambiguity rather than reducing it. See the official Claude Code tools reference for the documented behavior of Read, Edit, and Write.

questions.question: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports. The report-generation subagent follows the required section headings, but its judgment varies across runs when deciding whether a research claim should be stated confidently, qualified as limited evidence, or omitted. The handoff data already includes source URLs, publication dates, and evidence excerpts, and the output format itself is not failing validation. What change would most effectively improve consistency in this judgment?

choices.text: Add many unrelated report examples so the subagent sees a wider range of writing styles.
Add a stronger instruction that the subagent should be conservative and only include high-confidence findings.
Enforce a JSON schema for the final report-generation step.
Add 3-5 XML-wrapped examples that show relevant claim-evidence cases, edge cases, and ideal report phrasing.

explanations.A: Examples should closely mirror the real use case and cover relevant edge cases without teaching unintended patterns. Unrelated examples can add noise and may steer tone or structure in ways that do not match the research-report task.
explanations.B: This relies on subjective terms such as conservative and high-confidence, which different runs may interpret differently. It does not demonstrate the desired boundary between similar cases, so it is less effective for improving judgment consistency.
explanations.C: Schema enforcement is appropriate when the system must reliably produce valid JSON matching a defined structure. The stated problem is not JSON validity or schema compliance, but inconsistent judgment about how to phrase or omit claims.
explanations.D: Few-shot prompting is well suited when the issue is inconsistent judgment rather than invalid structure. Relevant, diverse, structured examples help Claude learn the decision boundary between confident claims, qualified claims, and omitted claims.

questions.questionExplanation: When a model follows the required format but varies in judgment, few-shot or multishot prompting is often the right lever. Anthropic's prompt-engineering guidance describes examples as a reliable way to steer output format, tone, and structure, and recommends making them relevant, diverse, and structured. In this case, examples should show the exact research-report boundary the team wants: a claim supported by multiple credible sources, a claim supported by only one source that needs qualification, and a claim whose evidence is too weak or conflicting to include. XML tags matter because the prompt mixes instructions, examples, and variable research inputs. Wrapping examples in <examples> and each case in <example> helps Claude distinguish training examples from the live evidence it must process. A few well-chosen examples are better than a large pile of unrelated samples because the goal is to teach the decision boundary without introducing irrelevant patterns. Structured output mechanisms solve a different problem. If the requirement were that Claude must always return valid JSON matching a schema, enforcing a JSON schema would be the more appropriate mechanism. Here, the schema and provenance handoff are already working, so the highest-leverage change is to demonstrate the desired classification and phrasing decisions through examples. See Claude prompting best practices, Increase consistency, and Structured Outputs.

questions.question: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports. During a long research run, early document analysis identifies a domain-specific taxonomy that should drive the final report. After many searches, tool results, and revisions, later synthesis passes start organizing findings around generic categories and occasionally contradict the earlier taxonomy, even though the application resends the accumulated message history. What change would best improve reliability?

choices.text: Maintain a structured research state file with the discovered taxonomy and source mappings, then load it into later synthesis prompts.
Increase max_tokens for later synthesis calls and continue sending the complete accumulated transcript unchanged.
Enable prompt caching for the accumulated prefix so earlier findings can be reused without affecting the context window.
Add a synthesis instruction to avoid generic categories unless the full transcript explicitly supports them.

explanations.A: This preserves the most important findings in a compact, explicit form instead of relying on the model to recover them from a long accumulated transcript. Loading the structured state into later prompts makes the domain-specific taxonomy and provenance salient again during synthesis.
explanations.B: Increasing max_tokens changes how much the model may generate, not how reliably it recalls buried input. Continuing to grow the transcript can worsen context rot because accuracy and recall degrade as token count grows.
explanations.C: Prompt caching can reduce cost and latency for repeated content, but it does not remove cached content from the context window. Cached input still contributes to the model's working context and does not solve buried-information salience problems.
explanations.D: This instruction may help in some cases, but it still depends on the model finding the relevant earlier facts inside a degraded long context. It does not create durable, structured state for the taxonomy or preserve claim-source mappings across synthesis steps.

questions.questionExplanation: Long-running research systems need to distinguish between having information somewhere in the request and making the information usable at the moment of synthesis. Anthropic describes the context window as the model's working memory and documents context rot: more context is not automatically better, and accuracy and recall can degrade as token count grows. A structured research state file, or scratchpad, keeps the discovered taxonomy, key claims, and source mappings compact and explicit so the coordinator can place them where later subagents will reliably use them. The Messages API is stateless, so the application is responsible for assembling the relevant messages, summaries, tool results, and synthetic state on every request. Sending the entire history unchanged may preserve bytes, but it does not guarantee attention to early findings, especially after many tool outputs and revisions. Prompt caching is useful for repeated prefixes, but the Context windows documentation states that cached tokens still count toward the context window, so caching is not a remedy for context degradation. The Working with messages documentation explains the stateless message model that makes application-managed context preservation necessary.

questions.question: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate. Production transcripts from a support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK show that after long conversations involving multiple orders, the agent sometimes applies a refund amount from one issue to a different order after older turns have been summarized. What change would most effectively preserve the critical issue details across the session?

choices.text: Summarize the complete conversation more frequently and replace prior summaries whenever the context grows large.
Maintain a structured case facts block that is updated after each relevant turn and made available on every relevant turn.
Add a system instruction telling the agent to remember all order IDs and refund amounts throughout the case.
Place the most recent order lookup result at the end of the prompt before the agent responds.

explanations.A: More frequent summarization can reduce token usage, but it increases the risk that exact details are compressed, paraphrased, or lost. This is the progressive summarization trap, where repeated summaries dilute the nuance needed for accurate multi-issue handling.
explanations.B: This preserves critical transactional facts outside the summarized conversation history, so details like order IDs, amounts, statuses, and decisions survive long interactions. In an Agent SDK deployment, session persistence and automatic compaction help manage context, but exact issue state should still live in a durable structured layer the agent can use when making decisions.
explanations.C: A system instruction can encourage careful behavior, but it does not create reliable durable state for exact transactional facts. If the relevant facts have been summarized away, compacted, or omitted from the agent's working context, the model cannot reliably recover them from an instruction to remember.
explanations.D: Recency can help the agent attend to the latest issue, but it does not preserve facts across multiple concurrent issues. It may also bias the agent toward the newest order while losing the relationship between earlier orders, amounts, and statuses.

questions.questionExplanation: For long, multi-issue support sessions, the safest pattern is to separate critical case state from the conversational transcript. A structured facts block can track fields such as customer_id, order_id, disputed amount, refund status, customer statements, policy decisions, and unresolved issues. The orchestration layer updates this block as new evidence arrives and makes it available to the agent whenever decisions depend on those exact facts, rather than relying on older dialogue turns to remain salient. The raw Messages API is stateless, meaning each API request must contain the information needed for that request. The Claude Agent SDK provides higher-level session persistence and automatic compaction, so an SDK application is not managed exactly like a hand-rolled Messages API loop. Even with those SDK features, compaction and summarization are lossy for precise transactional details, so refund decisions should not depend on compressed prose alone. Prompt instructions and recency tricks can improve behavior, but they do not provide a durable context layer. Summarization is useful for low-value dialogue and broad narrative history, while exact issue data should be represented as structured state that your orchestration layer owns. See the Messages API for the underlying request model, Claude Agent SDK for SDK-level agent session management, and Context windows for guidance on managing information within Claude's finite context.

questions.question: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports. In a test run, the coordinator executes the search and document analysis subagents, sends their tool_result blocks, then receives another assistant response with stop_reason: "tool_use" requesting the synthesis subagent. The current loop instead treats that response as the final answer and passes its text to the report generator, producing reports with missing synthesis. What change should you make?

choices.text: Continue the loop whenever stop_reason is "tool_use", return matching tool_result blocks, and use the response only when stop_reason is "end_turn".
Inspect the coordinator's assistant text for phrases like "ready to synthesize", then decide whether to run another subagent.
Send the synthesis subagent result as a tool_result block with a new tool_use_id, then resume report generation.
Run exactly one additional coordinator turn after every tool_result message, then treat the next response as the final report input.

explanations.A: This implements the documented client tool loop for the Messages API. A response with stop_reason set to "tool_use" is not the final answer, because Claude is requesting the application to execute one or more tools and return results.
explanations.B: Assistant text is not the reliable control signal for tool loops. Claude can include text alongside tool requests, so parsing natural language can cause the application to mistake an intermediate tool request for a final answer.
explanations.C: Tool results must match the original tool_use block by using its tool_use_id. Creating a new identifier breaks the required association between Claude's requested tool call and the application's returned result.
explanations.D: A fixed number of follow-up turns assumes the workflow shape in advance and can still stop while Claude is requesting another tool. The loop should be controlled by stop_reason, with iteration caps used only as safety guards rather than the primary completion signal.

questions.questionExplanation: In a client-executed tool loop, stop_reason is the application's control signal. stop_reason: "tool_use" means Claude has successfully stopped because it wants the application to run one or more tools, not because it has finished the task. The application should execute each requested tool, append the assistant tool-use message and the corresponding user tool_result blocks, then call the Messages API again. The normal successful completion state is stop_reason: "end_turn", which means Claude finished its response naturally and the application can use the assistant's final content. This distinction matters in multi-agent orchestration because a coordinator may need several rounds of subagent delegation before synthesis and reporting are complete. Fixed turn counts and text parsing are common loop-control anti-patterns. They confuse workflow assumptions with model state: Claude may need zero, one, or many tool rounds, and it may emit explanatory text in the same response as tool requests. Tool-result formatting also matters: for client tools, the assistant message contains tool_use blocks, and the next user message contains matching tool_result blocks with the correct tool_use_id. See Handling stop reasons, How tool use works, and Handle tool calls for the documented loop and message structure.

questions.question: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and understand when to use plan mode vs direct execution. After a long codebase analysis, this team wants to compare two alternative test-generation strategies from the same discovered baseline. Each investigation should preserve the baseline context, avoid contaminating the other strategy's reasoning history, and leave the original analysis session available for later use. What should the team do?

choices.text: Resume the baseline session ID with fork_session enabled for each strategy and run each investigation in a new session.
Duplicate the project folder twice and rely on each copied folder to contain an independent session history.
Resume the baseline session normally and ask Claude to keep each strategy in a separate section of its answer.
Continue the most recent session in the directory twice and assign each strategy a different prompt label.

explanations.A: This creates separate sessions that start with a copy of the original session history while leaving the original session unchanged. It is the right fit when two investigations need the same accumulated context but should diverge independently.
explanations.B: A session is accumulated conversation history written to disk, not a filesystem snapshot of the project. Copying folders may separate files, but it is not the documented SDK mechanism for branching a session history.
explanations.C: A normal resume continues the original session rather than creating a new branch. Prompting Claude to separate sections may organize the response, but it does not isolate the accumulated conversation history.
explanations.D: Continuing uses the most recent session in the current directory rather than a specified baseline session. It would not create isolated branches from the same known history, so one strategy's turns can affect the next investigation.

questions.questionExplanation: Use session forking when you want multiple investigations to start from the same accumulated context and then diverge. In the Claude Agent SDK, a session contains the conversation history, including prompts, tool calls, tool results, and responses. The documentation distinguishes continue, resume, and fork: continue finds the most recent session in the current directory, resume targets a specific session ID, and fork creates a new session that begins with a copy of the original session history while leaving the original unchanged. For Python SDK usage, the relevant option is fork_session on ClaudeAgentOptions, used when resuming from a specific session so the new work receives a new session ID instead of continuing the original. The important mental model is that this branches conversation state, not the project filesystem. If the investigations will also make code changes, you may still need normal development isolation such as branches or worktrees, but that is separate from preserving and branching Claude's session history. See the official session behavior in Claude Agent SDK sessions and the Python option reference in Claude Agent SDK Python.

questions.question: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems. During validation, the system described above calls a client-side lookup tool to find matching document IDs in an internal archive. Production traces show that tool timeouts and successful searches with no matches are both returned to Claude as `tool_result` blocks containing an empty array, causing the agent to treat access failures as confirmed absence. What change would most reliably preserve the distinction for downstream handling?

choices.text: Return no-match lookups as successful empty results, and return timeout failures as error tool results with retry context.
Use the successful Messages response `stop_reason` to infer whether the archive lookup should be retried.
Return both no-match lookups and timeout failures as successful empty results to keep the extraction schema simple.
Return both no-match lookups and timeout failures as error tool results to force conservative human review.

explanations.A: A successful query with no matches is valid information and should remain a successful tool result. A timeout is an execution or access failure, so the coordinator needs explicit error context to decide whether to retry, use an alternate path, or report a coverage gap.
explanations.B: The `stop_reason` field describes why Claude stopped generating after a successful Messages API response. It is not the same category as an archive access failure, an HTTP timeout, or a client tool execution error.
explanations.C: This suppresses access failures by making them indistinguishable from valid empty results. The agent and downstream systems lose the information needed to make retry or coverage decisions, which is a reliability anti-pattern in multi-step extraction pipelines.
explanations.D: This overcorrects by treating valid absence as a failure. It would route normal edge cases into error handling or review workflows unnecessarily, reducing precision without improving the system's ability to distinguish actual access failures.

questions.questionExplanation: The important reliability boundary is between valid negative evidence and missing evidence due to failure. A lookup that successfully returns no matches tells the extractor something meaningful: the queried archive did not contain a match under that query. A timeout tells the extractor something different: the system does not know whether a match exists, because access failed before the query could complete. For client-side tools, tool execution results are returned as tool_result blocks, and is_error should be used for execution errors rather than for ordinary empty results. In practice, the timeout result should include enough structured context, such as the attempted query and whether partial work occurred, so the coordinator can retry, try an alternate lookup, or annotate a coverage gap. The successful no-match case should remain a normal result, for example an empty list or a structured object indicating zero matches. This is separate from successful Messages API termination. Anthropic documents stop_reason values such as end_turn, tool_use, max_tokens, and pause_turn as reasons generation stopped after a successful response, not as transport or archive access failures. HTTP/API failures such as 504 timeout errors, 529 overloaded errors, and 429 rate limit errors are documented separately as error responses with an error object and require error handling rather than being collapsed into empty business results. See Errors and Handling stop reasons.

questions.question: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and understand when to use plan mode vs direct execution. A payments platform's developer productivity team is adding a /find-callers command that should locate every reference to a renamed helper function, limit the search to TypeScript source files, and return enough context for a developer to jump directly to each match. Which Claude Code built-in tool configuration should the command use?

choices.text: Use `Glob` with `pattern: "**/*helperName*.ts"`, sort the returned paths, and treat matching filenames as caller locations.
Use `Grep` with the helper name as `pattern`, scope with `glob: "**/*.ts"`, and set `output_mode: "content"` for matched lines.
Use `Glob` with `pattern: "**/*.ts"`, then `Read` each file and load all contents into the conversation for scanning.
Use `Bash` to run `grep -R "helperName" --include="*.ts" .`, then parse stdout as caller locations.

explanations.A: `Glob` finds files by filename or path pattern, not by text contained inside files. It would miss references in TypeScript files whose names do not include the helper function name.
explanations.B: `Grep` is the built-in Claude Code tool for searching file contents, which is what call-site discovery requires. Setting `output_mode` to `content` returns matching lines with file and line number, giving developers enough context to navigate to each match.
explanations.C: Reading every TypeScript file can consume unnecessary context and makes Claude do broad scanning manually. The dedicated content-search tool can find matching lines directly without loading full files first.
explanations.D: Running a shell command through `Bash` is not the same as using Claude Code's built-in `Grep` tool. The built-in tool has its own name, schema, output modes, and integration points for Claude Code configuration.

questions.questionExplanation: Grep is the Claude Code built-in tool intended for searching file contents, such as function names, error messages, and import statements. In this case, references to a renamed helper function are content inside source files, so the search should be expressed as a Grep pattern rather than a filename lookup. Glob is the right tool when the goal is to find files by path or filename pattern, for example **/*.test.ts. For developer navigation, Grep with output_mode: "content" returns matching lines with file and line number, and the tool can scope content searches with a glob filter such as **/*.ts. Avoid confusing the built-in Grep tool with invoking the shell command grep through Bash. The built-in tool has documented behavior and configuration surfaces in Claude Code, while shell commands are handled separately through Bash permissions. See the official Claude Code tools reference and Claude Code permissions documentation.

questions.question: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems. During evaluation, this team asks Claude Code to use subagents to investigate extraction errors across 600 vendor invoices, intake forms, and contracts. The current approach gives each subagent the same instruction, "find causes of schema validation failures across all documents," producing repeated observations and a large synthesis context. What change best partitions the investigation while preserving synthesis quality?

choices.text: Assign overlapping document subsets to multiple subagents, ask each to find any schema issue, and reconcile duplicates afterward.
Ask every subagent to review the full corpus independently, compare their repeated findings, and merge common schema issues.
Assign each subagent a distinct document group or extraction concern, provide needed context, and require concise findings for synthesis.
Create one nested subagent chain per document type, require verbose summaries at each level, and synthesize the final outputs.

explanations.A: This uses real subagent delegation, but overlapping scopes still create redundant investigation work. It also pushes duplicate findings into the synthesis step, which is the context-management problem the team is trying to reduce.
explanations.B: This can improve agreement checks, but it intentionally duplicates the same research path across all subagents. It also increases main-context pressure because each subagent reports similar detailed findings back to the caller.
explanations.C: This uses subagents for independent investigations, which is the pattern they are best suited for. Clear scope boundaries reduce duplicate work, while concise return formats limit how much subagent output flows back into the main conversation.
explanations.D: Nested subagents are supported, but this design adds unnecessary orchestration depth for independent research. Verbose summaries at each level also work against the goal of minimizing context growth and can obscure distinct findings during synthesis.

questions.questionExplanation: Claude Code subagents are useful when the main agent needs focused side investigations without filling the main conversation with raw search, log, or file output. The documented parallel research pattern is to spawn multiple subagents for independent investigations, then have the main conversation synthesize their results. In a structured extraction system, that usually means dividing work by document family, source type, schema section, failure mode, or another boundary that makes each research path non-overlapping. The important design tradeoff is that subagents have isolated context, but their final results still return to the caller. That isolation helps keep exploratory work out of the main thread, but it does not make returned output free. If many subagents send long reports, the main synthesis step can still become bloated, so each delegation should include the necessary context, explicit scope boundaries, and a compact deliverable format. Giving every subagent the full corpus is a plausible reliability instinct, but it primarily creates redundancy rather than better partitioning. Assigning overlapping subsets has a similar weakness, because it uses valid subagent delegation but fails to create clean scope boundaries. See Anthropic's documentation on Claude Code subagents for the documented isolation, delegation, and parallel research behavior.

questions.question: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems. This team is using the Messages API MCP connector with separate MCP servers for schema selection, entity enrichment, and delivery to a downstream queue. They want one extraction request to choose tools from all three integrations as needed, rather than preselecting a single integration per document. What should they implement?

choices.text: Define all three servers in mcp_servers only, omit mcp_toolset entries, and rely on automatic tool discovery across the connections.
Define all three servers in mcp_servers, add one matching mcp_toolset per server in tools, and let Claude choose among the discovered tools.
Create one generic proxy tool, route every operation through it, and hide server-specific tool metadata from Claude.
Run three separate requests, each with one mcp_toolset, and pass extracted JSON between requests manually.

explanations.A: For the Messages API MCP connector, mcp_servers alone is not sufficient to enable tools. The request must also include a corresponding mcp_toolset entry in the tools array for each configured server.
explanations.B: This matches the documented Messages API MCP connector configuration for multiple MCP servers in one request. Each server connection is defined in mcp_servers, and each must be referenced by exactly one MCP Toolset so its tools can be enabled for Claude.
explanations.C: This removes the tool descriptions and schemas that help Claude select the right capability reliably. A generic proxy can also make validation and routing harder because Claude no longer sees distinct tools with clear names, descriptions, and input schemas.
explanations.D: This unnecessarily fragments the extraction flow and prevents Claude from selecting among all relevant tools within the same request. MCP supports connecting to multiple servers, and the connector supports multiple MCP servers when each has a corresponding MCP Toolset.

questions.questionExplanation: MCP is designed around a host, client, server architecture in which an AI application can connect to more than one MCP server. The architecture documentation describes fetching tools from all connected MCP servers and combining them into a unified tool registry available to the language model, while routing each tool call back to the server that owns that tool. With the Messages API MCP connector, the request shape matters. Defining servers in mcp_servers establishes connection details, but enabled tools are configured through {"type":"mcp_toolset","mcp_server_name":"..."} entries in the tools array. For multiple servers, include multiple server definitions and one corresponding MCP Toolset for each server. This design lets Claude choose among schema, enrichment, and delivery tools based on tool names, descriptions, and schemas within a single extraction request. Splitting the workflow across separate requests or hiding the tools behind a generic proxy gives up the MCP discovery model and usually reduces tool selection reliability. See MCP architecture, MCP tools specification, and Anthropic MCP connector.

questions.question: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and understand when to use plan mode vs direct execution. This team is creating a project-scoped /investigate command for unfamiliar codebase questions such as "why are refunds sometimes double-counted?" and "where should we add tests for the importer?" The command will use a coordinator that can delegate independent investigations to subagents before proposing a plan. Which prompt design best preserves adaptability while keeping the output reliable?

choices.text: Specify a fixed sequence of repository scans, file reads, grep patterns, test commands, and final report sections.
Define the investigation goal, evidence requirements, output format, tool/source guidance, task boundaries, and effort budget heuristics.
Ask each subagent to research the requested area broadly, avoid constraints, and return any useful observations.
Assign every request to the same frontend, backend, database, and testing subagents before synthesizing results.

explanations.A: This design over-constrains the coordinator by making the same procedure apply to every investigation. It is more like a predefined workflow than an adaptive orchestrator-workers pattern, so it may miss paths that only become relevant after initial findings.
explanations.B: This design gives the coordinator enough structure to delegate useful work without freezing the investigation into a fixed path. It aligns with dynamic orchestration because the coordinator can choose subtasks based on the specific code question while still enforcing quality criteria and bounded effort.
explanations.C: This design is too vague to support reliable delegation. Without an objective, boundaries, expected format, or source guidance, subagents are more likely to duplicate work, misunderstand scope, or leave important gaps.
explanations.D: This design uses predetermined subtasks even when the user’s question may not involve those areas. It can waste effort and reduce relevance because the coordinator is not deciding the decomposition from the actual input.

questions.questionExplanation: For an agentic codebase investigation, the coordinator should be guided by goals and quality criteria, not a brittle recipe. Anthropic distinguishes workflows, which follow predefined code paths, from agents, which dynamically direct their own process and tool use. A prompt that fixes every scan, command, and subtask can unintentionally turn an adaptive investigation into a rigid workflow. The orchestrator-workers pattern works because the coordinator determines subtasks from the input, delegates to specialized workers, and synthesizes their findings. Good delegation still needs structure: each task should include an objective, output format, tool or source guidance, and clear boundaries. Effort budgets, such as scaling the number of subagents and tool calls based on task complexity, are useful because they bound work without dictating the exact path. This is especially important for Claude Code workflows where unfamiliar codebase questions vary widely. The same /investigate command might need dependency tracing, test gap analysis, data flow inspection, or log-driven debugging depending on what the coordinator discovers. See Anthropic’s discussion of agents and workflows in Building effective agents and its lead-agent/subagent research architecture in How we built our multi-agent research system.

questions.question: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems. The repository has packages for invoices, contracts, and claims, each with different extraction edge cases and validation conventions. Developers usually start Claude Code from the package they are editing, and maintainers want package-specific standards loaded automatically without making every package inherit every domain's guidance. What configuration best fits this workflow?

choices.text: Move all domain standards into the root CLAUDE.md and separate them with headings for invoices, contracts, and claims.
Place @ imports for every standards file inside a fenced code block in each package CLAUDE.md.
Keep shared conventions in the root CLAUDE.md and let each package owner add @ imports for only that package's relevant standards in its package CLAUDE.md.
Store each package's standards in separate Markdown files and link them from package READMEs instead of importing them.

explanations.A: This would make every domain's standards part of the always-loaded root context for all package work. Headings improve readability, but they do not make Claude Code selectively load only the relevant package guidance.
explanations.B: Import parsing skips Markdown code spans and fenced code blocks. Putting @ imports inside a code block would show them as literal text rather than expanding and loading the referenced files.
explanations.C: This uses the documented monorepo pattern of layering root instructions with per-package CLAUDE.md files. The @ imports are organizational includes, and when Claude Code starts in a package directory, the package file and its ancestors are loaded while sibling package files are not loaded at launch.
explanations.D: Claude Code uses CLAUDE.md for persistent instructions and supports imports from CLAUDE.md using @path syntax. Keeping standards in separate Markdown files can help documentation organization, but linked files are not automatically loaded as package memory unless they are imported or otherwise read.

questions.questionExplanation: For a monorepo, the practical pattern is to keep repository-wide conventions in a root CLAUDE.md and place stack-specific or package-specific guidance in each package's own CLAUDE.md. A package maintainer can use @path/to/import entries to include the standards files that actually apply to that package, for example invoice extraction rules in an invoice package and contract clause conventions in a contracts package. The important mental model is that @import organizes memory content, it does not make imported files lazy or free. Imported files are expanded and loaded into Claude's context alongside the CLAUDE.md that references them. Selectivity comes from where the import is placed and where Claude Code is launched: starting in a package directory loads that package's memory plus ancestors, not sibling package memories at launch. Use care with paths and Markdown formatting. Relative imports resolve relative to the file containing the import, and an import written inside backticks or a fenced code block is treated as literal text. To verify the result, /memory can show which memory files are loaded in the current session. Relevant documentation: Claude Code memory and Claude Code large codebases.
